We introduce the concept of single-photon quantum optical catalysis to describe light-field state transformations achievable through multi-photon nonlinear processes, initiated by a solitary photon. A primary characteristic of this phenomenon is the ability to generate high-dimensional coherent superpositions, such as those involving two-photon Fock components, using just one photon. We illustrate these ideas using specific neutral-atom interaction models and explore the implications for advanced phase measurement techniques, including single-photon catalyzed homodyne and interferometric methods. Furthermore, we detail the formation of single-photon catalyzed coherent phases and propose a Fock-interferometric scheme employing such phases for precision phase detection.

Defining bivectors in General Relativity may initially seem unnecessary, especially when working with component-based methods like tensors in Cartesian coordinates or the Newman-Penrose formalism itself. However, adopting this approach within that framework yields significant advantages. This work introduces a new definition of the electromagnetic field bivector using only complex numbers. It further explores the impact of this construct on both the interpretation and computational handling of the Weyl tensor and the electromagnetic field. Notably, the author discovers a previously unidentified relationship between these fields and the self-dual and anti-self-dual volume orthogonal bivectors relative to any null tetrad. Finally, it is demonstrated within this framework that both real electromagnetic field invariants and all components of the Weyl tensor can be expressed through the aforementioned bivectors.

The linear regression technique, widely recognized for its effectiveness, remains underutilized in the inference of polymers. We infer a polymer $\mathcal{P}$ by solving a linear regression task, where the target variable is defined by monomer counts in a target string $y$, and the features $X$ represent the counts of each distinct monomer within $y$. We demonstrate that this approach infers a generator containing only one instance of any monomer that occurs exactly once across all training sequences. Furthermore, we establish a connection between linear regression and the 0-1 integer programming problem, showing that while regression offers close approximations, the 0-1 integer programming formulation yields optimal polymers. We introduce this method to the sequencing community, emphasizing that it is conceptually simple, computationally efficient, and easily adaptable to other inference tasks. Experiments on synthetic and real sequencing datasets confirm that the proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques, achieving a significant improvement in F1-scores of over $30\%$.

During the drilling process, operators aim to maximize the production of hydrocarbon reservoirs by optimizing the well trajectory. Because formation evaluation data from well logs is acquired concurrently with drilling, geosteering engineers utilize this real-time input to make dynamic decisions regarding the well path. Given that both the logs and their application in interpreting subsurface properties involve inherent uncertainties, this study introduces a framework for uncertainty quantification within well log analysis. The approach is demonstrated using examples of uncertainty propagation from resistivity and density logs, which are employed to estimate formation permeability and porosity. Results indicate that this methodology effectively quantifies uncertainty in real time, enabling engineers to assess the confidence levels of their decisions made while actively drilling.

The framework is designed to align with annotator tendencies and the inherent nature of these entities while remaining straightforward to implement. Empirical assessments utilizing the recently introduced CoSNER dataset—which comprises a dedicated collection of nested named entities and pairs for these entities—demonstrate that our method outperforms strong baselines.

This paper examines a technique for target node estimation in Wireless Sensor Networks (WSN) that suffers from interference caused by devices operating on the same frequency. This approach utilizes the readings of two technologies coexisting within the network to achieve a localization precision unattainable by either technology in isolation. A three-dimensional analytical model, accounting for mutual interference, is proposed to determine the positions of nodes. The inherent complexity of the interference precludes standard analytical solutions, making analytical geometry and computational methods necessary alternatives. To address this, an innovative, easy-to-implement geometric algorithm has been developed. Its high computational efficiency and practicality make it suitable for deployment in resource-constrained microcontrollers. The study validates the algorithm's precision and practicality through MATLAB simulations and a physical testbed, demonstrating that it delivers a precise localization solution. Results indicate that the proposed interference-aware solution outperforms current interference-agnostic approaches, successfully integrating into real-world WSN deployments.

Multilingually active communities frequently utilize more than one language within a single sentence, a phenomenon known as code-switching (CS) and the resulting input, code-mixed (CM) natural language processing (NLP). However, developing resources and models for these code-mixed environments remains difficult due to the infinite variability of language pairs, inherent lack of structure, and scarcity of annotated datasets. Despite these obstacles, such models are vital for preserving sociolinguistic identity and enabling inclusive NLP. This paper reviews key areas in CM-CS NLP, including language identification, tokenization, named entity recognition, question answering, sentiment analysis, and document and event grounding. We also examine existing multi-lingual CM-CS models, explore influential factors like data scarcity, model capacity, and evaluation strategies, while offering future research directions to advance multilingual inclusivity in NLP.

Automatic description generation for images has become a standard component of general purpose AI systems, serving as a significant area of research. This approach leverages large, annotated datasets comprising both images and corresponding descriptions to train models capable of generating similar narratives. A critical research question is whether humans genuinely evaluate these outputs, or if apparent high scores result from participants simply matching their inputs to available labeled examples. To investigate this, we conducted a user study where 100 Amazon Mechanical Turk workers evaluated descriptions generated for images from the Flickr30k dataset. These inputs included a baseline of ground truth descriptions from that same dataset, as well as descriptions created by large neural networks trained on Flickr30k but applied to Microsoft Research's Sub2015 dataset. The results indicate that human preference for generated text over ground truth descriptions varies significantly depending on the training data of the model used. Furthermore, we analyzed a subset of inputs where users favored automatic generation to identify characteristics of these cases, revealing that current models excel at describing images containing humans engaged in activities. However, these systems still frequently rely on matching user selections of provided labels, suggesting that while human evaluation remains a valuable research metric, care must be taken to utilize appropriate and diverse datasets.

Tantalum oxides (Ta$_2$O$_5$) are renowned for their unique ability to undergo reversible insulator-metal phase transitions (IM-PT) triggered by external stimuli such as temperature changes, light exposure, or electrical fields. These dynamic phase transition properties make them highly valuable for applications in phase-change memory, memristors, and memtranist technologies. Although traditional methods like neutron and x-ray scattering have been employed to characterize these materials, their limited temporal and spatial resolution often struggle to capture the fast, stochastic nature of the transition. To address this gap, we conducted a combined study using *ab-initio* calculations and Monte Carlo simulations. This approach enabled a detailed examination of the transition's underlying physics and a precise mapping of the ground-state lattice structures of both the insulating and metallic phases. Our findings reveal that the insulating state is defined by a quadrupolar phase, whereas the metallic state corresponds to a charge density wave. Furthermore, the research highlights that the transition mechanism is governed by a Ginzburg-Landau-type dynamics driven by a specific metallic intermediate state.

This large-scale empirical study examines the propagation of misinformation regarding a specific news event within the news section of Reddit, utilizing a dataset of 33.8 million account activity logs and 52.8 million Reddit posts and comments to trace 15 instances of information spreading (both accurate and false). The primary objective is the 36-hour circulation of the top-hyped rumor, dubbed the "Main Event Rumor," which garnered 15.8 million interactions across 282,000 unique users from January 11 to 13, 2021. Analyzing the behavioral patterns of Reddit users sharing this top-polarized misinformation reveals three distinct chronological phases: an initial introduction via inbound traffic from external platforms, an internal expansion marked by circulation across diverse subreddits, and a final decline driven by users returning to external activities. To effectively model and understand misinformation dissemination, we introduce a novel framework termed the Big Geographic Shift (BGS), representing a migration of the content from outside the platform into its internal ecosystem followed by a reverse movement back outside. We further explore the intricate connection between user polarization and this BGS phenomenon to enhance a comprehensive grasp of how misinformation propagates.

Accurate anomaly detection is fundamental to safeguarding modern networked systems. Nevertheless, the recent surge in the volume of data transmitted over the internet, driven by the widespread adoption of high-speed connectivity, presents significant challenges for existing methods. Current techniques typically rely on statistical analyses of distributed samples, which necessitates that most protocol packets be inspected. Such an approach is often impractical given its high overhead, particularly in environments where infrastructure is constrained. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a lightweight, practical framework designed to identify anomalies within restricted sampling contexts by leveraging the protocols' inherent structural knowledge. Empirical evaluations conducted on mirrorings of the Internet's backbone and a research facility network demonstrate that our method effectively identifies anomalies with superior accuracy and substantial computational efficiency compared to prior state-of-the-art solutions.

Human demonstration serves as a fundamental method for task learning, with speech playing a critical supportive role. This study examines acoustic characteristics of speech during human task execution to identify potential criteria for automatic, real-time detection of demonstration phases. Specifically, we analyzed acoustic profiles across three communication contexts: voluntary offers of assistance, requests for assistance, and task execution involving speech. Our findings reveal that voluntary offers to demonstrate tasks through speech exhibit distinct acoustic characteristics compared to other contexts, notably differing significantly from requests for assistance. Additionally, we observed distinct acoustic separations between performing a task with speech and asking someone else to do so. Demonstrating statistical validation via an listener experiment, these results indicate the distinctiveness of scenarios where a task is demonstrated through speech versus when assistance is sought or provided collaboratively. Finally, a robotic manipulation system was developed to independently segment task demonstration phases based on these identified speech characteristics.

The paper proposes a novel algorithm to generate $T_n$, defined as a random mixed-type tree of order $n$ according to the specific recursive structural rules provided. These rules dictate that for $n > 1$, a tree $T_n$ forms by rooting two sub-trees, $T_k$ and $T_{n-k}$, drawn recursively from the set of valid trees of lower orders (where the index $k$ is chosen based on a defined probability distribution), and combining them. The author establishes the convergence of the algorithm and investigates a property regarding $T_n$: as $n$ approaches infinity, the probability that any given specific order-$n$ tree is produced by the algorithm converges to a limit, thereby confirming that all valid trees of order-$n$ are generated with strictly positive probability.

We introduce a novel formulation of the Euler-Arnold equation on $\mathfrak{s}\mathfrtables2,\mathbb{R}\}\}$ that streamlines the connections between these fields. Specifically, we establish a new correspondence connecting Liouville conformal field theory, Virasoro shadows, and Riemann $\chi2,\mathbb{C}\}$. As a result, we derive a closed, non-perturbative expression for the non-toroidal partition function of the free boson on a negative metric. Additionally, we determine the precise non-perturbative corrections affecting the three-point correlation functions of the same bosonic system. Finally, by leveraging the Riemann $\chi2,\mathbb{C}\}$, we calculate the Virasoro spherical punctured surface metric exactly, while also deriving a closed-form result for the four-point correlation functions of the unitary case.

Conversational agents, functioning as interactive software that dispense information and execute tasks, have gained significant popularity. An effective automated testing framework for these agents is essential to guarantee their reliability and stability in the wild. However, existing frameworks fall short because they cannot simultaneously address the need for flexible human involvement and the efficiency of full automation. Introducing the "ConviTest" system, a novel framework designed to ensure agent robustness and reliability by bridging this automation-human input divide. Researchers can utilize framework features like modular design, diverse interaction modes, screenshot generation, and automated message sending to create extensive test case suites. Offers comparative analysis demonstrates how the system supports both automation and human interaction, along with practical deployment of framework for testing the "TiGi" agent.

Various theories suggest a massive Planet X exists in the distant solar system, potentially responsible for orbital biases among known planets. This study investigates whether the hypothesized orbital wobble caused by Planet X is observable in the precise astrometric data currently available. We specifically analyzed both the long-period cometary orbits and the trajectories of major planets, including Pluto, Neptune, Saturn, and Eris. Our findings indicate that even without advanced modeling of non-gravitational forces, the influence of Planet X is detectable in the orbital paths of long-period comets. Furthermore, its signature is clearly identifiable in the orbits of the four largest planets. We estimate that a single astrometric dataset provides sufficient constraints to pinpoint Planet X's semi-major axis ($a_{1/2\pi}$) and eccentricity ($e_{1/2\pi}$) within a $1\sigma$ uncertainty range of approximately $30$ degrees for both parameters. We also examined the orbital wobble of Mars, Mercury, and Jupiter, concluding that while Planet X could be identified in datasets dedicated to long-period comets or giant planets, astrometric models limited to a single dataset are likely insufficient for detecting its gravitational effects on Mars, Mercury, or Jupiter.

Translating text requires effective access to vocabulary from the source language to the target language. While current translation models often utilize vast bilingual dictionaries, they frequently fail to adequately reflect how human translators operate by relying on monolingual knowledge. To address this, we introduce a new **Lexicon Memory** module that enables machines to learn from extensive unaries (monolingual) texts. This module updates its internal state based on the current and predicted words, effectively capturing linguistic patterns. By integrating this module into a Neural Machine Translation framework and training on both bilingual and extensive monolingual data, we demonstrate that the system can significantly improve translation accuracy. Specifically, using the same amount of bilingual training data as standard models, our approach outperforms them by a full 1.1 BLEOU point on the newstest 2014 benchmark when trained on additional monolingual data. Furthermore, our model achieves superior accuracy using 50% less bilingual data compared to standard models trained on identical data.

Within the framework of Conformal Cyclic Cosmology, which posits an eternal succession of universes where Hawking's black hole evaporation enables metric rescaling to link them, we examine potential imprints on the cosmic microwave background (CMB) arising from cosmological anomalies. Specifically, we address two observations: first, the alignment of temperature anomalies with Hawking radiation signatures from evaporated supermassive black holes in prior universes, a scenario that may account for certain CMB features; and second, the calculation of statistical probability distributions regarding the spatial arrangement of temperature anomalies and those of primordial gravitational waves. Additionally, we explore implications for the cosmic neutrino background. Although these cosmic signatures remain undetected in the current universe, their presence in earlier epochs could offer explanatory value for the observed cosmic microwave background anomalies.

This paper extends a recent finding by the author and C.V. Sarnath, which demonstrated convergence of the fractional flow associated with the Yamabe problem toward a stationary solution. Originally, this work showed stability for rational eigenvalues. Here, we elevate the proof to cover a broader spectrum, establishing it for measure-supported eigenvalues as well. Consequently, this generalization allows us to conclude data-independent convergence for the fractionnal Yamabe Yambe problem.

Few-shot learning focuses on rapidly acquiring new capabilities by leveraging minimal data. In this study, we introduce a novel few-shot learning algorithm designed to identify and instantiate a small number of prototypical examples for each class. A key innovation is the dynamic determination of prototype dimensions based on the actual data, as these sizes are treated as latent variables inferred alongside model parameters. This approach enables prototypes to function as high-dimensional clusters, where a cluster head is inferred to represent an entire group of similar items. A distinctive feature is the use of a single shared stochastic neural network head for generating prototypes across all classes, regardless of whether data for those classes exists in the support or query sets. This architectural efficiency allows the model to be trained entirely on a single source domain and deployed effectively for querying entirely different, unseen classes.

In contemporary e-commerce ecosystems, recommendation performance is significantly hampered by data sparsity, a scenario exacerbated in multi-sparse domains where both users and items lack sufficient interaction information. Addressing this challenge, we introduce a novel framework termed Multi-Sparse-Domain Cooperative Recommendation (MSDRC). This approach leverages information across domains to enhance recommendation within a single sparse domain; however, it employs aspect-based knowledge from other domains to mitigate data sparsity specifically, rather than applying raw cross-domain information directly. Central to the MSDRC framework is Enhanced Comprehensive Aspect Preference (ECAP) learning, which synthesizes multiple latent user and item aspects from diverse sources. Crucially, ECAP dynamically regulates the incorporation of latent information from various domains based on relevance, ensuring effective recommendation within the target domain. Extensive experiments conducted on two real-world datasets validate the superiority of the proposed MSDRC framework.

The **Hypatia.jl** package enables the formulation and resolution of natural conic problems using standard linear algebra operations and differential operators. While conic optimization offers significant advantages over conventional convex methods—such as reduced variable counts, lower dimensionality, and the preservation of problem structure—libraries supporting the cone paradigm (like the **Sol** package in R or **SCIP**) often require labor-intensive manual variable substitutions and constraint generation. In contrast, **Hypatia.jl** facilitates the direct solution of natural conic systems, a capability that supports specialized **Hypatia.R** functions for solving specific system types. This approach supports a broad spectrum of cone types, including positive definite, semidefinite, and order cones associated with polynomials, rational functions, and polynomials over finite fields. By ensuring computed solutions inherently adhere to the necessary conditions for conic optimality, **Hypatia.jl** further supports efficient natural solvers, such as the dedicated **Lode** package for direct factorization.

Automated quality assurance systems are increasingly utilized to detect artifacts in MRI scans prior to analysis, yet they struggle with slow generalization when encountering new centers or specific pathology types. To investigate these limitations, we examined MRI black artifact detection using data from three centers, covering both healthy individuals and patients with brain diseases. Although an ensemble of three deep supervision U-Net architectures achieved near-perfect detection on training data (F1 score = 0.99), the performance dropped sharply on test sets (F1 score = 0.38). This initial model failed to capture the test sites' dominant positive class—brain tissue—and incorrectly classified large healthy brain regions as artifacts. Furthermore, supervised pre-training on a proxy task, "distinguishing brain from non-brain images," initially worsened performance on the primary task. However, employing a two-stage approach where the network is first trained on the proxy task and then fine-tuned on the target task significantly boosted test performance (F1 score = 0.62). Ultimately, the success of this multi-task strategy suggests that the model's difficulties stemmed from insufficient exposure to the diverse variations of brain structures present in healthy and diseased populations.

Extreme weather events are increasingly disrupting electricity supply, leaving vast populations without power. While widespread outages are often driven by extreme weather, the subsequent recovery process can be further slowed by uncoordinated vehicle charging demands. This study investigates the synergy between vehicle and load recovery after such events, specifically examining how a surge in private electric vehicle (PEV) recharging influences the efficiency of restoring both systems. To capture this dynamic, we propose a resilient charging framework that coordinates a massive number of autonomous, privacy-conscious PEVs to optimize charging schedules. By focusing on this heterogeneous, large-scale population of vehicles, we aim to ensure efficient grid recovery alongside load satisfaction.

This paper presents comprehensive performance evaluations of the Intel DC Persistent Memory Module, a form factor utilizing the DDR4 DIMM shape but offering main memory with storage-level durability. While manufacturers promote potential applications for memory-intensive database workloads, empirical validation through real-world scenarios remains limited. Consequently, this study conducts extensive micro-architectural analyses to differentiate between system behaviors during DRAM and PMem access patterns. Subsequently, we configure databases utilizing Optane DC PMem in various ways to evaluate actual performance implications. Our findings offer performance insights into database systems operating with Optane DC PMem, highlighting both opportunities and constraints. Ultimately, we observe that although Optane DC PMem delivers substantial bandwidth and latency, current database implementations often fail to fully utilize these capabilities effectively.

While the current study focuses on a specific setting, the proposed framework is designed to be broad in scope, allowing reasoning structures to support a range of motivations and goals within diverse contexts.

This study presents image analysis methods designed to identify tumors within MRI data. Key features extracted from these images serve as input for multiple machine learning algorithms, including Naive Bayes, K-Nearest Neighbors, Support Vector Machine, Decision Tree, Random Forest, and Neural Networks. Automated data aggregation in wireless sensor networks (WSNs) involves two critical tasks: determining link transmission priorities and estimating link quality. Existing approaches often rely on random or fixed hierarchical structures, which fail to optimize the "read" process, while their quality estimation methods lack bidirectionality, potentially missing essential information. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel, demand-driven framework. This approach employs a **Bidirectional Link Quality Estimation (BLQE)** algorithm alongside **Hierarchical Range Partitioning (RNG)**. The RNG method dynamically divides the monitored area into tiers based on the collection needs, optimizing the use of multi-hop communication. The BLQE algorithm assesses nodes from both directions to ensure comprehensive and efficient data aggregation. Rigorous analysis and experimental results validate the efficiency and performance of this proposed system.

This study examines the dependence of the hadron production asymmetry on the sum of the partons' helicities in the SIDIS scattering event when both proton spin states are longitudinally polarized. A detailed theoretical framework is established for this phenomenon, with calculated results presented within the leading-order (LO) collinear factorization formalism, specifically focusing on the dihedron fragmentation process. The paper explores the origin of this asymmetry through the mechanism of dihedron fragmentation and offers a viable strategy for experimentally determining certain strong interaction coupling parameters. Furthermore, the theoretical predictions are contrasted against available data from the SLC and HERA accelerators.

This work lies at the intersection of Combinatorial and Commutative Algebra, with our focus primarily on the Macdonald coefficients emerging from the expansion of Macdonald symmetric functions. We present several findings that enhance the "conjectured symplectic characterization" associated with Macdonald coefficients. Specifically, we introduce a fresh combinatorial framework grounded in the interaction between affine and classical Weyl groups, utilizing it to redefine the symplectic combinatorial objects previously conjectured. Furthermore, we establish a new finding linking the non-zero entries of symplectic matrices of type B to specific combinatorial traits of monomial symmetric functions, while also deriving an explicit formula for computing these entries.

This study constructs layered Wikipedia-based entity recommendation models to generate diverse and high-quality recommendations for Knowledge Graph (YAGO) entities. Due to the scarcity of suitable organ donors, numerous individuals with end-stage renal disease must rely on dialysis, while there is a pressing necessity to evaluate and integrate kidneys deemed too large for their recipients. This study addresses the dynamic allocation of oversized kidneys to patients whose standard match would otherwise take excessive time to materialize. We introduce a stochastic framework for this specific context and derive the criteria for an asymptotically optimal dynamic policy by leveraging a scaled semi-discrete time approach that yields an asymptotically equivalent continuous-time model. Subsequently, by demonstrating the regularity of the total cost in our asymptotic schema and applying Varadhan's asymptotic large deviation principle to asymptotic costs, we establish the convergence of any cost-minimizing dynamic strategy to an optimal limit. Finally, we assess an incremental "vanishing mismatch" heuristic in numerical simulations, finding it produces costs only marginally higher than those of the optimal asymptotic policy.

Also known as unsupervised learning, implicit ties represent the dominant paradigm in contemporary machine intelligence. This survey outlines the principles, objectives, and inherent constraints of implicit training, while providing a comprehensive classification and review of recent advancements in this field.

NLP initiatives frequently leverage word polarity embeddings to analyze financial documents, with polarities serving as foundational inputs for constructing broader sentiment classification schemas. Although polarities are instrumental in financial text analytics, this study investigates whether contemporary word embeddings genuinely internalize these nuanced classifications. Using three distinct analytical methods, we challenge current language models, which often rely on generic, context-agnostic pre-training. Specifically, we assess the polarities of pre-trained contextual representations through a majority vote mechanism and the Kullback-Leitner distance metric, while also training a contextual model exclusively on news text labeled with sentiment. Our analysis reveals that while models like ELMa demonstrate a propensity to align with sentiment labels, they lack the precise granularity and consistency found in the original source texts. Furthermore, we observe that BERT and Word2Vec exhibit inconsistent tendencies to reflect these polarities. Ultimately, our results indicate that word2vec and BERT do not inherently grasp the specific "Loughran-McDonald polarity" framework, even though ELMa shows some implicit understanding.

In contrast to current deep learning methods for multiplayer games, which focus on finding strong strategy profiles like Nash equilibria while offering minimal to no explanations, this study introduces a system that simultaneously determines a Nash equilibrium and generates a shared visual and textual interpretation acceptable to all players. Our approach builds upon recent initiatives in collaborative explanation generation and addresses a distinct challenge: creating individualized explanations for specific arguments within a Nash equilibrium that remain consistent with their mutual justification. Evaluated against top-tier current methods on standard collaborative explanation benchmarks, our model is verified to be more powerful at delivering high-quality, coherent, and reliable justifications. Source code is available at https://github.com/zheng-pan/xneq.

This study examines the spread of epidemics on networks that incorporate preventive rewiring, a mechanism where susceptible individuals rewire uninfected connections at a specific rate to avoid potential exposure. Although the various networks in the study are inherently random, they all support nontrivial epidemics and are analyzed using a stochastic model for individual dynamics and a corresponding deterministic mean-field approximation. Results indicate the presence of a backward bifurcation in the networks, meaning the basic reproduction number ($R_0$) alone does not determine the threshold for epidemics. Instead, a second threshold emerges, where the stable disease-free state shifts to an unstable bistable region before supporting endemic equilibria at higher infection levels. This bistability is further explored through the application of probabilistic techniques to assess the likelihood of epidemics in the individual stochastic framework.

In the domain of reinforcement learning, where agents interact with dynamic environments to refine policies maximizing expected returns, diversification within data reuse often mirrors financial investment strategies. Within the context of Deep Q-Learning (DQL), this concept manifests as "Experience Replay," which fetches training transitions at random from a stored buffer, thereby promoting data variety. Nevertheless, conventional sampling methods rely on stochasticity alone, failing to guarantee optimal diversity despite its intent. To bridge this discrepancy, we introduce "Div-Replay," a variance-reduced diminishing diversity algorithm that efficiently retrieves highly diverse batches with minimal statistical variance. By integrating this approach as a core component of DQL, we achieve a resulting model exhibiting superior intelligence and performance metrics. Empirical evaluations through both simulated benchmarks and physical robotics platforms substantiate these findings, confirming the method's efficacy.

Determining the electronic and superconducting gap structures of iron-based superconductors is essential for validating various microscopic theories. In this study, we employ high-resolution angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) to investigate the $(\text{Ba}_{0.6}\text{K}_{0.4})\text{Fe}_2\text{As}_2$ sample, which exhibits a single superdoming at the $X$ symmetry point in its electronic structure. Our analysis reveals $s^{\pm}$-wave symmetry as the correct configuration for describing both the electronic and superconducting gap structures, explicitly disproving the previously suggested $d$-wave symmetry. Furthermore, by integrating ARPES data with density functional theory (DFT) and scattering theory, we determine a gap amplitude ratio of approximately $2.3$ between the $\Gamma$ and $X$ directions. Notably, spin-flip magnetic exchange interactions derived from DFT calculations align well with the mechanisms proposed in the standard $s^{\pm}$-wave scenario.

Recently, a generalized form of the hubbard-Stratonovich transformation, along with the superbosonization equation, has been introduced to manage the nonlinear Dirac equation with Yukawa interactions. In this work, we analyze a specific case of the nonlinear Dirac equation with scalar interactions in three dimensions, applying both the generalized transformation methods to compare and contrast their approaches. The results indicate that utilizing the generalized transformation yields a local form of the generalized bosonization equation, whereas applying it to the circual form produces a local version that corresponds precisely to a localized form already obtained through the generalized method. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the two methods yield physically consistent outcomes when both are applied in their respective local representations.

This paper reports a measurement of top quark polarization in $t$-channel single top quark production using datasets collected by the CT equick detector at the Large Hadron Collider (CERN). The analysis employs inverse weighted estimation derived from simulated samples featuring varying levels of top quark polarization to quantify this level among real data events. The simulation employs a mixed-event technique combining unlabeled real and simulated events to produce "hybrid" top quark polarization values. The technique's accuracy and reliability are tested using different combinations of real data and Monte Carlo simulation. The final result, derived purely from hybrid simulations, achieves approximately 1% statistical precision and combines 4% systematic uncertainty. The measured top quark polarization value is found to be consistent with predictions from the Standard Model.

Using $\beta$-detected NMR with radioactive $^{8}$Li, we examine the electronic structure of LaNiO$_3$ and LaNiO$_3$/${\rm LaAlO}_3$ superlattices. The study reveals a continuous evolution of the magnetic and conducting states as the NiO$_3$ layer thickness decreases. While bulk LaNiO$_3$ features a characteristic antiferromagnetic spin gap, our results show that even a single unit of monolayer thickness induces metallic behavior coupled with the closure of the spin gap. Furthermore, increasing the number of NiO$_3$ monolayers to three causes the re-emergence of long-range magnetic order and the opening of a spin gap, even when a conducting LaAlO$_3$ interface is present. These findings indicate that the interplay between metallicity and magnetic ordering in these systems can be manipulated through the thickness of the individual layers.

We introduce MultiTalk, a dialogue testbed designed to explore and evaluate diverse conversations through a highly branching structure. Although current dialogue systems excel at simulating specific behaviors like small talk, deception, or providing medical advice individually, they lack a platform for concurrent diverse interactions. Addressing this gap, our system supports eight distinct but overlapping conversational styles, allowing a dialogue system to interact with all simultaneously. To facilitate this, we developed an efficient alignment mechanism that defines the structural framework of the testbed. Results indicate that dialogue systems achieve significantly higher perplexity when engaging MultiTalk compared to their respective baseline dialogues on four specific scenarios: small talk, social chit-chat, deception, and advice-giving. Furthermore, we observed that dialogue systems demonstrate decreased generational coherence and quality when participating in MultiTalk. We believe offering such a resource will advance the field of dialogue research.

Correlation is considered in both the IRS correlation and the antenna correlation. Additionally, the study proposes a realistic model of the phase-shift of the IRS in order to enhance throughput. In order to analyze the throughput of the system, the study derives its throughput of the system. Conducting full $N$-body simulations in modified gravity (MG) remains challenging, particularly when the modifications are non-linear and generic. We introduce a suite of full $N$-body MG simulation software designed to numerically evolve a general class of conformally coupled models. In this framework, the MG stress-energy tensor is constructed by combining a modified dark energy stress-energy tensor adhering to the Einstein equivalence principle with ordinary baryonic and cold dark matter (CDM) components. We employ an adaptive time-stepping integrator to ensure accuracy across the entire spectrum of expansion histories, from the early to the late times of the universe. This approach allows for significant flexibility in implementing various parameters associated with the MG stress-energy tensor. Specifically, the code supports multiple forms of the modified dark energy equation of state, distinct barotropic parameters for various matter fluids, and explicit functional dependencies for the Einstein frame potential, which is constrained by the Einstein equations. To address the efficiency of modeling the Einstein frame, the authors implement a specific parametrization of the Einstein frame potential, which is determined by the specified equation of state and the Einstein frame potential's evolution. This approach allows for significant computational savings in locating the minimum of the Einstein frame potential, which is required for the simulation. The validity of the implementation is confirmed by reproducing previously published results. The authors demonstrate the utility of the code by running their first simulations of this kind for a specific, physically motivated form of the modified dark energy equation of state

Finally, following E R-SLE's methodology, we show how specific radii in E R-SLE's enable the calculation of these GF F's via multi-SLE correlation functions.

This study investigates the acoustic behavior of turbulent jet flames within a linearized analytical framework. Specifically, it models the reaction of a turbulent, buoyancy-supported methane/air jet to its own acoustic field. Initially, an active flow theory is simplified to apply in the passive limit, yielding a linearized flow model validated against experimental data for non-forced jets across various velocities and temperatures. Subsequently, this methodology is adapted to represent flame-induced acoustic instabilities by integrating linearized flame-induced heat release rates. Two primary heat release models are evaluated: a conventional Markstein flame response and a newly suggested, more sophisticated reaction formulation. Results indicate that while both models capture general flow and acoustic characteristics, only the advanced reaction formula accurately predicts primary acoustic modes and associated mode shapes. Furthermore, this enhanced model accounts for the secondary acoustic modes generated by jet-sheath vortex shedding, demonstrating superior overall capability in this context.

The lack of detected ultra-high-energy (UHE) extragalactic photons flux, specifically for energies exceeding 1 PeV, presents a significant challenge. One potential mechanism to explain this observation involves the absorption of such Isotope photons within the Earth's atmosphere or another attenuating process, although in this specific work we investigate the contribution from the Earth's magnetic field. We demonstrate that our model, which incorporates inverse-Compton scattering between UHE photons and static, quantized (spin-1) virtual ones in an isotropic model of the Earth's field, successfully reproduces the observed flux limitations for UHE photons. Additionally, we note that we have established a novel link between this high-flux component and the structure of the Earth's magnetic field.

Nonlocal theory of gravity constitutes a viable alternative to general relativistic framework. In this study, we investigate the fundamental frames and constitutive relations within a monotonically developing nonlocal gravity model. Our analysis establishes that the interplay between fundamental frames is governed by a dissipative hyperbial process, indicating that nonlocal gravity operates within fundamental regimes as a dissipative system. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the hyperbial evolution of these parameters serves as a unique hyperbial constitutive relations, which are distinct from the standard hyperbial constitutive relations of special holes.

Distributed systems often utilize replicated data to enhance performance and resilience, employing replication policies that allow concurrent writes for high write throughput. However, unregulated concurrent writes can lead to write waste, where later operations overwrite and discard earlier ones, as many current data structures lack mechanisms to prevent this inefficiency. Observing that real-world systems address such concerns through abstractions like conflict-free replicated data types (CRDTs), which eliminate this waste by design, we note the current limitation where CRDT implementations rely on ad-hoc, context-specific approaches. To resolve this, we introduce **Remove-Win**, a modular framework for constructing removal-winning CRDTs within a consistent architecture. Frameworks are provided for foundational collections, maps, sets, counters, and functions, with modules available to integrate custom ordering functions. By enabling the construction of conflict-free replicated data types that preserve capability for removals, the framework facilitates the development of "removal-winning" CRDTs, ensuring both consistency and the ability to execute and undo operations effectively.

Genomic association studies and annotation of genomic features are essential for identifying genes related to specific traits and understanding their underlying biology. Although association studies can detect variants linked to traits and explain biological mechanisms, they do not always yield significant associations for every trait. Consequently, integrating multiple data sources to enhance the analysis of associations is increasingly important. This study presents a joint modeling approach that combines genome-wide association studies with annotations of genomic functional data to estimate the prior probability of a variant being associated with a specific trait. We applied this method across twelve diverse phenotypes, demonstrating improved statistical power in detecting associations for eight traits, including obesity, height, and systolic blood pressure, and identifying novel associations for autism spectrum disorder, obesity, and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol levels.

This work reviews the properties of these minor systems, outlines current research efforts, and identifies promising avenues for future investigation.

The evolution of the Milky Way's central supermassive black hole is likely driven by accretion luminosity from neutron star (NS) x-ray binaries, which periodically approach close to it. Observations suggest that many x-ray pulsers in the galactic center reside in long-term transient states, cycling between accretion outburbreaks and periods of inactivity. We propose a mechanism where these events occur when a companion star migrates inward due to dynamical interactions, bringing it within the NS's Roche lobe. This scenario explains why these systems are detected as transients rather than stable donors. Furthermore, the timescales between successive transients align with expectations for binary formation via direct capture from the stellar merger pool. These x-ray pulsers are accreting from stars slightly more massive than those in the old, well-populated globular clusters. Consequently, the resulting x-ray luminosity from these transient events is sufficient to sustain an x-ray background that mimics a central black hole actively accreting from a reservoir of Eddington-limited material, consistent with findings by Robertson et al. (2012).

The wide binary star method involves analyzing the orbital motions of wide binary systems to discriminate between competing theories of gravity. This approach was initially suggested by Khanna (2000) to differentiate General Relativity from MOND and has since been enhanced by later investigations. This work aims to broaden the wide binary framework by identifying and assessing numerous prevalent and niche alternatives to General Relativity, incorporating scalar-tensor, Einstein-aether, Hoava, cubic scalar theories, $f(R)$ gravity, and emergent cosmology models. According to the refinements proposed in this study, the method's sensitivity sensitivity is sufficient to detect deviations as minor as 1%, potentially around 0.1%, provided observations yield precise measurements of orbital semi-major axes and period lengths. However, the approach encounters substantial obstacles: orbital periods for wide binaries are excessively lengthy, necessitating exceptionally long baselines of astrometric data to gather sufficient observations. Consequently, the utility of wide binaries as a laboratory for gravity depends critically on whether upcoming astrometry missions, such as Gaia 3, can successfully achieve the requisite data precision.

The stacking technique is a statistical approach that aggregates numerous radio sources sharing identical redshifts to investigate their properties, particularly when individual measurements remain obscured by significant noise. Employed here to examine the spectral indices, ionization states, and morphological structures of large samples of 1.4 GHz radio sources at $z=2.0$, this method was applied to data from the ATLAS-2D survey. High-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) serves as a premier technique for visualizing and characterizing the microscopic structural variations of paraelectric perovskites. Using BaTiO₃ as a model system, we developed an automated approach to generate simulated HRTEM images based on first-principles calculations. These simulations accounted for atomic positions derived from the five competing structural prototypes—specifically the tetragonal $P4mm$ and the orthorhombic $Cmcm$, $Cmcm$, $Cmcm$, and $Cmcm$—along with their respective antiphase domain boundaries (APBs). By optimizing imaging conditions, such as the defocus parameter, through which these materials are typically observed in experiments, we achieved accurate lattice fringe patterns for both bulk regions and structural interfaces. Furthermore, by applying statistical analysis to atomic position data within each parent structure and their APBs, we successfully recreated the characteristic features seen in experimental observations, including variations in fringe visibility and contrast, as well as atomic displacements along the [001] zone axis. Consequently, this efficient, simulation-based method offers a practical means of realistically modeling the HRTEM signatures of structurally similar, microscopic inhomogeneities found in other strongly correlated, strongly correlated, and other similar materials. Conventional diffraction-based analysis often falls short in this regard, often failing to capture the necessary structural detail.

We present predictions for the experimental observation of a novel theoretical strongly correlated Dirac metal. In this phase, simultaneous symmetries breaking of both lattice and chiral states allows correlation effects to significantly alter the Dirac semimaterials. Specifically, we forecast that the linear dispersion of a Dirac semimaterial would evolve into a scaled linear or anti-fermionic fermionic dispersion following symmetry breaking. Additionally, if the degree of scaling is sufficient to open a gap in the electronic structure, a correlated insulating state would emerge. We specifically examine the case of Bismuth, demonstrating that the exact combination of symmetry breakings could yield this new correlated Dirac metal phase. In the resulting gapless state, unique phenomena are anticipated, including non-trivial magnetotransport characteristics and a spontaneous staggered magnetic order. Furthermore, if the gap opens, substantial modifications to optical properties would result. Discovering and analyzing this novel phase would provide a valuable platform for investigating the interplay between spontaneous lattice and chirality breakages in determining fundamental electronic behaviors.

The standard binomial distribution serves as a foundational model in Bayesian statistics for characterizing uncertainty in unimodal binary data. However, in practice, binary data often arises from two distinct populations with differing characteristics, necessitating a framework that can express uncertainty about both the group-specific parameters and the grouping itself. To bridge this gap, we introduce the Bimodal-Bernoulli distribution, which functions as a comprehensive prior for such scenarios by defining probability masses for both binary outcomes and the associated variances within each modal group. We demonstrate the utility of this approach through a case study involving postoperative pain management and antidepressant response rates, comparing single models against integrated models with specific structures for each response category.

Heavy Neutral Leptons (HNLs) represent a compelling Heavy Neutrino scenario capable of accounting for anomalies observed in lepton flavor universality and meson mixing. This study examines the sensitivity of CERN's ongoing NA62 experiment regarding the decays $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$. We evaluate how current electron flavor neutral current (LFU) ratios, specifically $\mathcal{R}_{e2}$ from NA62 and $e^- N$ from PIP-II, constrain the decay $K^+ \to \pi^+ HNL$. We find enhanced sensitivity in the mass interval $200 < m_{HNL} < 400~\text{MeV}$, where existing limits are dominated by the $\mathcal{R}_{e2}$ ratio. We estimate that with an equal or greater number of protons delivered, NA62 could achieve a $3\times$ improvement in the existing limits for this mass range.

We examine the spectral shift anomaly reported by Resch and Padgett, involving Gaussian laser beams traversing a closed loop within a Sagnac interferometer, where a spectral shift is observed when the entire system rotates about an axis aligned with the interferometer's axis of rotation. While previous studies attribute this shift to the mechanical Bernoulli effect caused by centrifugal force within the looping structure, we propose instead that the shift originates from a relativistic Bernoulli effect resulting from the transformation between the global Galilean frame and the rotating frame of the instrument. Furthermore, we analyze a scenario in which the axis of rotation is offset from being collimated with the axis of the loop, a configuration that yields additional spectral shifts.

This article explores the structure of the parabolic adjoint operation $A_0(\mathfrak{g}, B, \lambda)$, defined as a specific fibre within the nilfibre (where entries belong to the Borel subalgebra of $\mathfrak{sl}_n$). We examine cases where the nilfibre's dimension equals $A_0(\mathfrak{g}, B, \lambda)$, and explore the structuring of elements within this operation into sections resembling Weierstrass forms, as well as a partitioning process resembling a Niltiber partition.

Although language models represent the cornerstone of natural language processing, the widespread shift toward fully neural architectures has pushed out earlier methods like $n$-gram language models. This transition occurred despite $n$-gram approaches offering the state-of-the-art in Chinese Word Segmentation and Information Extraction tasks at the time. We reinstate the $n$-gram language model as a textual preprocessor to facilitate neural-based tasks, introducing a residual language framework that adapts neural networks to mirror the strengths of $n$-gram models. Employing this framework in Chinese processing yields performance improvements across multiple downstream activities.

Given a Laurent series $f \in k((t))$ with coefficients in a field of characteristic zero, the Laurent series inversion performs a transformation on $k(t)$ that converts rational functions into algebraic elements within the formal power series field $k[[t]]$. We establish an analogous transformation acting on the coordinate rings of $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano varieties and $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano complete intersections within $k[[t]]$. Specifically, this operation transforms an element algebraic in the formal power series ring $k[[t]]$ into a member of the defining parameter set for a new $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano variety or complete intersection, respectively, whose graphically reflected singularity spectrum strictly dominates the original. As a consequence, we identify a novel mechanism to generate families of new $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano varieties and complete intersections, with applications extending to the study of mirror symmetry.

We introduce a new 3D dense face alignment and reconstruction system known as Self-aligned Dual Face Regression Networks (SADRNet). This network processes both the frontal camera view and a synthesized 3D folded face image to produce high-precision 3D dense alignment. By employing both image domains, the method effectively mitigates the ill-posed nature of monocular face analysis. The framework functions as follows: the frontal camera stream recovers the initial approximate head pose, orientation, and shape through a 3D face regression network, while a dedicated 3D folded face processing module finalizes the dense alignment and reconstruction tasks. This architecture enables end-to-end training and analysis. Extensive experiments confirm that the proposed approach outperforms current state-of-the-art methods on two leading benchmarks, demonstrating its effectiveness.

Our research examines how the dissemination of music through streaming platforms can inadvertently facilitate the distribution of harmful pathogens embedded in file names or metadata. While existing security measures effectively mitigate many cyber threats, they often fail to flag biological hazards because research into biological attacks lags behind studies on cyberattacks. Furthermore, current automatic file classification systems generate a high volume of false positives by rejecting known risky content, which can lead to the censorship of benign material. To address this, the goal is to minimize both cyber- and bio-bore injections without sacrificing security or free expression. The proposed solution integrates a specialized vocabulary of benign words and a novel biological co-occurrence network, which maps potential biological references in filenames against established safe terminology. This approach was validated using a dataset comprising 1.5 million song titles from metadata and filenames, along with 1,000 labeled examples of biological content drawn from 13 distinct pathogen categories and nine malicious agent types. Results indicate that for bio-bore injections, the system achieves a 99.9% recall rate, correctly identifying over 99% of cyber-bore injections, while rejecting fewer than 0.1% of non-malorous content.

This study examines a model where storage service providers offer their capacity in an environment of potentially fluctuating rates. Specifically, it analyzes the optimal strategy for a single vendor to allocate storage given specific risk preferences, considering both current and future market conditions. An analytical framework is established to characterize these allocation decisions under varying levels of asset liquidity and market volatility. Furthermore, a comparative analysis explores how risk aversion influences the chosen storage strategies. The paper concludes by introducing a novel approach allowing storage capacity to function as collateral for a loan, analyzing the resulting optimal allocation when financial leverage is considered.

The completion of atomic and molecular dynamics within the attosecond era enables new frontiers in science, particularly regarding the creation of superpose states of electrons in both energy and momentum space. Nevertheless, current capabilities for electron-specific timing resolution remain restricted. Here, we demonstrate the generation of highly correlated, coherent electron-momentum states by illuminating platinum metal with intense, ultrafast XUV pulses. This approach results in the synchronization of multiple core-hole excitation sites, inducing competitive resonant and non-resonant decay pathways that significantly influence the charge state distribution of the ejected electrons. By competitively tuning these pathways, we shift the coherent electron dynamics occurring on a sub-Auger timescale, specifically altering their level of coherence. This study not only surpasss existing spatial resolution limits for electrons but also establishes novel methodologies for engineering electron-based attosecond wavepackets.

We analyzed the dynamics of planetary atmospheres using simplified global climate models. By systematically varying parameters such as surface friction, heat exchange, and Coriolis effects, we identified a continuous spectrum of circulation patterns that shifts from geostrophic turbulence through zonal banding to equatorial cyclostrophic super-rotation. This progression mirrors both laboratory experiments with rotating fluid annuli and observations of terrestrial and Jovian planetary atmospheres. Specifically, we identified the transition from geostrophic to super-rotational regimes as the exchange of momentum variability timescales, which in highly super-rotating systems is dictated by the planetary scale, with less exchange in the intermediate regime. We found that surface heat exchange primarily influences the latitude and intensity of these circulation bands, whereas surface friction dictates the transition between geostrophic turbulence and super-rotation. Additionally, we observed that in the simplest configurations, atmospheric turbulence is triggered by a single control parameter, while more intricate setups require at least two parameters to cross the transition threshold.

We introduce an approach to large-scale visual recognition training that enables continuous, experiment-quality adaptation to new ImageNet 100k images using fully stochastic methods. Achieved through a novel algorithm named Hinge-S, which integrates controlled high-speed updates with a specific rejection mechanism for suboptimal parameter changes, our method ensures a robust training dynamic. Tests indicate that Hinge-S generates outputs comparable in standard deviation to those from standard training procedures but executes five to fifty times faster. Additionally, when applied to the 100k dataset with a Gaussian kernel, Hinge-S facilitates the creation of a powerful 100K-ImageNet 100K (100K-ImageNet 100K) visual recognition benchmark, supporting the training of Gaussian models that achieve state-of-the-art results on this dataset.

This note investigates analytical and geometric characteristics of the characteristic polynomial $\chi_A(t)=\chi_A(A,t)$ of a complex square matrix $\chi \in \mathbb{C}^{n \times n}$. A primary focus is placed on the algebraic multiplicity $m_A(\lambda)$ associated with an arbitrary scalar $\lambda \in \mathbb{C}$. The paper presents several novel findings, including the derivation of new formulas for $m_A(\lambda)$ utilizing values of $\chi_A(t)$ and its derivative $\chi'_A(t)$ evaluated specifically at $\lambda$. Furthermore, geometric interpretations of $m_A(\lambda)$ are explored through the lens of manifolds formed by matrices possessing prescribed spectra. The results establish that $m_A(\lambda)$ equals the codimension of the orbit $\mathcal{O}_A$ of matrix $A$ (under unitary transformations) within the general linear group $\mathcal{GL}_n$, as well as through the analysis of level sets of eigenvalue multiplicity functions. These findings collectively offer fresh perspectives on $m_A(\lambda)$, including those relevant to the Jordan structure of $A$. Finally, the paper discusses connections between $m_A(\lambda)$ and the multiplicities inherent to eigenvalues.

We theoretically examine the generation of correlated bosonic pairs and the emergence of squeezing within a system of long-lived electric dipo interacting with an optical cavity. Specifically, we investigate the scattering of photons from two to within the sub-terahz and microwave frequency ranges, a process characterized by distinct correlations and spatial squeezing of the photons. We observe that the magnitude of this squeezing is highly dependent on the frequency of the scattered bosons and the specific arrangement of the dipoles. Furthermore, we demonstrate the utility of these tightly correlated, spatially squeezed photons for enhancing high-precision optical phase measurements.

Donor spins in silicon are a promising candidate for quantum computing, yet simulating their dynamics is computationally demanding. We present a modified multi-valley effective mass approach that accurately captures donor electron and hole eigenstates by fully including valley mixing. By integrating this method with Efimov's analytical formalism for donor spin states, we have performed comprehensive simulations of a triple-arsenic donor complex in silicon. Comparisons with numerical plane-wave methods demonstrate that our proposed effective mass method achieves an accuracy of approximately $10^{-4}$ $\text{\AA}^{-2}$ while being roughly four orders of magnitude faster. Furthermore, we analyze the computational efficiency and applicability across various donor configurations and species. We also calculate the zero-field electronic degeneracy for multiple arsenen and phosphorus configurations, providing necessary parameters for subsequent donor spin simulation using the analytical multiv donor states within this new theoretical framework.

We analyze the theoretical transport characteristics of HgTe quantum films with a band gap, focusing on conditions leading to a non-zero critical temperature ($T_c$) where a Dirac mass gap emerges. Furthermore, we investigate a model incorporating finite gapless regions within the film to explore how they affect the mass gap and determine the conditions under which the system behaves as a conventional metallic conductor.

V2X communications at road intersections are essential for enabling vehicle platooning and safety-critical functions like collision avoidance and braking coordination. This study introduces a stochastic analytical framework to evaluate the throughput of infrastructure-assisted NOMA (I-NOMA) for unicast transmissions within V2R scenarios, comparing its results against orthogonal multiple access (OMA). Using a stochastic geometric approach, the analysis accounts for co-channel interference caused by successive NOMA decoding, which depends on node density, transmission power levels, and access list configurations. Simulation results validate the theoretical models and demonstrate that I-NOMA outperforms OMA in terms of throughput by approximately 37%. Furthermore, this geometric analytics-based analysis provides a robust foundation for designing efficient interference management and resource allocation algorithms for wireless networks supporting collision avoidance and braking coordination at intersections.

This study introduces a novel game-theoretic framework for scheduling TDD uplink and downlink subframes in the future of the fifth generation (5G). Within this model, each subframe functions as a contest where mobile users strive to maximize their data rates, while simultaneously, both users and the base station strategically select transmission formats to optimize transmission efficiency and total system capacity. By employing the Nash equilibrium concept, we analyze the stability of this framework. Furthermore, to achieve convergence toward efficiency optima, we propose a sophisticated best-response stochastic learning algorithm tailored for reinforcement. Convergence analysis confirms that this algorithm successfully achieves a near-Nash equilibrium state. Extensive simulations demonstrate that, compared to existing state-of-the-art TDD scheduling methods, the proposed game-theoretic approach significantly boosts total system capacity, enhancing data rates specifically for uplink connections.

Although the Hall anomaly observed in type-II superconductors is frequently ascribed to a Hall vacuum formed by vortices within a defect-rich lattice induced by valence vacancies, several features of the phenomenon remain difficult to reconcile with current models. In this study, we present strong evidence supporting the existence of this Hall vacuum by analyzing experimental datasets from BSCCO thin films in a rigorous manner. We demonstrate that the carrier density inferred from the anomalous Hall effect aligns precisely with the density of vacancies calculated from the impurity conduction threshold, whereas the standard vortex model yields a carrier density that is orders of magnitude higher and thus fails to match the findings. Furthermore, the vacancy framework accurately accounts for the non-monotonic temperature dependence of the anomalous Hall coefficient ($R_{xy}$) seen in the datasets, while the vortex-based approach offers no explanation for this specific behavior.

We examine how specific moment fixed points, as categorized by Vignale and Schmitz within their *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 103, 180602 (2009) publication, influence the three-dimensional Ising universality class. By numerically evaluating high-order moments and analyzing the resulting moment fixed points through the lens of Landau theory of phase transitions in light of V. L. Ginzburg's framework of fluctuation theory, we demonstrate that the Vignale and Schmitz identified fixed points do not contribute to the critical behavior of this system. Furthermore, we establish a connection between moment fixed points and droplet phases, showing that they correspond to non-critical behavior found in first-order transitions. Finally, our numerical findings indicate the potential emergence of a new class of fixed points associated with fluctuation-driven, first-order transitions.

Automated systems are increasingly integral to our daily activities, which has heightened public scrutiny regarding potential biases in machine learning models. This concern is particularly acute in high-stakes domains like healthcare and finance. While prior research has focused on detecting and mitigating unfairness, this study investigates how end-users interact with and influence automated decision-making. We identify that users frequently overlook unfavorable outcomes by engaging in reward-based interactions with positive predictions. Leveraging this behavior, we introduce a novel multi-agent framework that integrates trust scoring with trust data augmentation to enhance fairness and reduce bias. In a housing discrimination classification task, our method successfully diminishes bias by 30% to 60% and lowers unfairness metrics by between 17% and 33%. Our findings offer an accessible approach to improving fairness in both the inputs feeding these models and the models themselves.

Detecting contraband items in x-ray imaging is vital for safeguarding public safety, a task that has drawn extensive research attention. Nevertheless, significant challenges persist, including the difficulty of generating large-scale, high-quality negative sample datasets, the prevalence of overlapping objects, and variations in rotation and illumination. Although current methods relying on few-shot learning and attention mechanisms effectively address prohibited object detection in both visible light and x-ray domains, they often struggle with robustness against real-world complexities such as severe clutter, physical cluttering, and distinct environmental differences. To overcome these obstacles, this study introduces a comprehensive dataset comprising 100,000 images featuring 10,000 annotated prohibited objects across 1,000 categories. Additionally, we propose a Lateral Inhibition Module (LIM) designed to optimize the detection of overlapping objects by simulating the visual system's natural lateral inhibition response. This module dynamically suppresses activation levels in neural regions corresponding to background areas or objects outside the focal point, while enhancing activation for target contraband items. Our model integrates LIM within a few-shot learning framework specifically tailored for x-ray security, utilizing a spatial cross-attention structure to achieve a unified detection solution. The proposed spatial cross-attention framework, combined with the dataset, delivers state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance on both standard and challenging tasks involving high-difficulty contraband detection.

Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) stands as a significant challenge in natural language processing, tasked with identifying the appropriate word meaning based on surrounding textual context. This study introduces a new task known as Context-Gloss Disambiguation (CGD), which directs algorithms to select which definition of a gloss best fits a given context sentence. We developed a dedicated framework for this task and broadened it using both synsets from Microsoft's SenseList-19 (SL19) and context sentences drawn from Wikipedia. Our framework integrates multiple contextual embeddings enhanced by gloss features to amass a comprehensive corpus for CGD. Using only Wikipedia synsets, our framework achieved an F1 score of 79.02%, notably surpassing the adaptation of state-of-the-art WSD models, which reached just 63.92% when tested on our Wikipedia-based corpus. Furthermore, incorporating an external WSD knowledge base like SL19 improved performance to 87.22%. Notably, our method also outperformed direct adaptations of leading WSD models on the official GLAD 2019 benchmark dataset, hitting 80.08% (on a test subset) and 70.50% (on the complete set), respectively.

Typically, the $\Gamma$-function is defined by the integral $ \Gamma(z) = \int_0^\infty e^{-xt} t^{z-} dt $. In this paper, we derive a regularized version of this formula that is valid for all $z$ by the following relation: \[ \int_0^\infty (e^{-t}-e^{-xt}) t^{z-} dt = \Gamma(z)\rho(z)\], where $\rho(z)$ denotes the normalized reciprocal of the Ramanujan Q-function, often written as $1/\Gamma(z)\rho(z)=e^{\gamma z}/\Gamma(1+z)\]. We further provide a proof for the integral formula using a contour deformation method.

This study presents an investigation into top quark production within proton-nucleus collisions, utilizing inelastic p+p collisions as a reference framework. The calculation employs the pTCET framework, integrating parton distribution functions (PDFs) adapted for proton-proton interactions and those specific to the nucleus. The simulation accounts for both single and rare top quark events, incorporating the determination of the factorization and renormalization scales. A primary objective is to evaluate the suitability of pTCET for future proton-nucleus collisions at the Electron-Ion Collider (EIC).

Cross-domain text-to-SQL interpretation is a challenging task that demands significant effort to manually construct training data, particularly when aiming for large-scale datasets. This paper proposes generating difficult road networks for the validation of Automatic Emergency Lane Keeping Systems (ALKS) using a new, optimization-driven technique. The core of this approach is a specialized objective function that simultaneously enforces specific driving scenarios and ensures dynamic changes in road geometry. Constraints within this function guarantee adherence to physical limitations, including vehicle dynamics and roadway specifications. The driving scenario component forces the optimizer to identify solutions aligned with defined driving conditions, while the geometric variation element promotes diversity in the resulting test tracks. Through a gradient descent algorithm, satisfying all constraints yields valid road profiles. Once these profiles meet regulatory requirements, they are smoothed into continuous, drivable surfaces via cubic Bézier curves. Finally, scene objects are positioned relative to the generated topology to construct a comprehensive driving scene.

Using scene simulation and system-level evaluation metrics, we validate both the scene generation and resulting ALKS test cases. Our generated scenarios successfully create challenging and diverse situations that push vehicle controllers to their limits, effectively producing complex and varied road topologies. Consequently, this framework offers a promising foundation for the automated synthesis of rigorous test cases for advanced driver assistance systems.

Temporal action detection (TAD) focuses on identifying the beginning and ending of actions within a video. Although numerous methods have been developed to address this task using visual content and temporal knowledge, their effectiveness often declines when actions are obscured by background distractions or irrelevant foreground elements. Drawing inspiration from the importance of both local and global information, we introduce Dual Context Aggregation Networks (DCAN), a framework designed to enhance the aggregation of extensive long-term contextual data. Specifically, DCAN employs a Dense Clip-level Context Aggregation Network (DCCAN), which treats each video clip as a unit to capture context densely and intricately through a combination of dense dense convolutional networks. Additionally, it features a Anchor-based Anchor Aggregation Network (ACAN), which selects representative segments from each clip to synthesize context from multiple hierarchical levels. Furthermore, to further improve performance, we propose Multi-View Temporal Sampling (MVTS), ensuring a more comprehensive sampling of temporal information across varying granularities and directions. Experiments conducted on two distinct benchmarks confirm that DCAN surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques, highlighting its efficacy.

We report the detection of photon recoil effects in the optical absorption spectrum of an ultracold strontium vapor, observed directly using high-resolution, single-beam spectroscopy. A Lorentzian resonance centered on the transition from the strontium 5s atomic ground state to the excited 5s5p atomic P state exhibits significant modifications due to the momentum imparted to Sr atoms absorbing photons. Specifically, the resonance develops a photon recoil-induced dip and accompanying side peaks. These features persist even after subtracting the contributions from magnetite oscillations, implying that the observed spectrum is not merely a convolution of multiple physical phenomena. Instead, the distinct shape serves as definitive evidence of matter-wave dynamics within this system. Consequently, this finding underscores the necessity of incorporating atomic matter-wave models to accurately interpret high-precision spectroscopic measurements employed for determining fundamental physics constants.

Dramatic, sudden transitions in flow behavior characterize shear thickening, a phenomenon where material resistance increases as agitation intensifies. These events are relevant to numerous natural and industrial contexts, including volcanic flows, food manufacturing, and wearable armor technology. Although the rise in resistance during these events can be abrupt, the magnitude of this rise varies significantly by material, often spanning several orders. This study investigates the universal features of these transitions across diverse systems by aggregating experimental data from granular media, concentrated pastes, colloidal suspensions, and polymers. We examine how resistance evolves with agitational intensity, capturing both the magnitude of the sudden increase and its range. Our analysis reveals a consistent power-law relationship governing the universal scaling of these transitions, supported by a stochastic framework applicable to both granular and soft substances. Furthermore, we introduce a distinct parameter termed "softness" to differentiate soft matter from granular substances and propose an integrated theoretical model that unifies the mechanics of these two categories.
