In today's interconnected world, individuals and organizations constantly face the challenge of deciding whether to trust strangers. Research indicates that Internet and social media platforms can aid in establishing this trust, yet they also create new vulnerabilities by enabling the formation of deceptive identities. This paper introduces a new metric for assessing computer-mediated trustworthiness, known as the Density of Verifiable Connections (DoVC). The metric focuses on the proportion of connections that are publicly identifiable, such as mutual friends or professional contacts. Empirical analysis of LinkedIn profiles revealed that only 29% of connections qualified as verifiable on average, suggesting that even well-established accounts maintain sufficient DoVC to help users identify reliability. In contrast, randomly generated spam and phishing profiles scored significantly lower, with their connections largely unverifiable. Furthermore, experiments show that DoVC effectively distinguishes between trustworthy users and those engaged in cyberbullying. Collectively, these findings support the hypothesis that the metric functions as a robust tool for gauging trustworthiness in online interactions.

Normal Gaussian diffusion, characterized by a mean position evolving linearly over time and constant, homogeneous diffusion, represents the standard. In contrast, anomalous non-Gaussian diffusion is frequently observed in biological and other systems, marked by deviations in particle displacement time means or the absence of time-independent positional variance. This review investigates two specific mechanisms of randomness within the initial conditions or the diffusion process itself—either within the set of initial states or in the diffusion mechanism itself—leading to anomalous non-Gaussian behavior.

We present a straightforward yet rigorous matrix-based formalism that fully generalizes the standard theory of optical resonance, propagation within waveguides, and their nonlinear Kerr interactions. This formalism builds upon and extends the concepts of orthogonal and degenerate resonance modes, as well as Kerr frequency conversion. A fundamental innovation introduced is the concept of "Kerr-modes," which encompasses all resonance behavior modified by Kerr effects acting on any given set of resonance or propagation modes. Similar to traditional approaches, generalized orthogonal Kerr-modes exhibit orthogonal linear coupling and degenerate nonlinear self-oscillation, while other mode types correspond to non-orthogonal Kerr-modes with coupled nonlinear dynamics. This approach offers a fully general framework specifically tailored for analyzing and understanding the operation of all-Dioptical resonator systems.

This study introduces a super-resolution (SR) framework utilizing a generative adversarial network (GAN) to recover high-resolution velocity fields from low-resolution data of chaotic flows, covering Reynolds numbers from 100 to 2800. Two GAN architectures, specifically the Single-Stage Residual Enhancement Super-Resolution Network (RRSRN) and the Multi-Stage Residual Learning Super-Resolution Network (MRLSRN), were evaluated. The RLRSRN demonstrated superior performance against RRRSN, accurately reconstructing both flow field structures and SPOD amplitudes across the entire spectrum of Reynolds numbers examined. Uncertainty modeling stands as a critical challenge in modern machine learning, particularly within open-domain settings like automatic speech recognition (ASR) and search engine ranking. Currently, learning-based methods learn to calibrate confidence scores using supervised data, a constraint that prevents their use in open-world scenarios where labeled inputs are unavailable. To address this gap, we introduce a novel, self-supervised open-world uncertainty modeling framework that operates by monitoring the energy levels of unlabelled data. Specifically, we propose learning two distinct components: an energy-driven open-world uncertainty representation and an energy-to-confidence mapping function. Our method functions as a calibration layer situated between an uncalibrated base model and the ultimate output, effectively translating raw base model energies into reliable confidence measures. We evaluate our approach across three diverse tasks—ASR in open domains, language modeling, and learning-to-rank systems—demonstrating through extensive experiments that our method surpasses existing open-world uncertainty representations and exceeds strong baseline performance by a significant margin.

Although significant progress has been made in applying Reinforcement Learning (RL) across diverse tasks, exploring the field's overall advancement and pinpointing specific obstacles remains challenging. We address this gap by introducing **L2Explorer**, a specialized RL evaluation platform designed to facilitate continuous assessment and identify key barriers. Drawing heavily on the **LifeLong** structure, L2Explorer hosts a unified collection of benchmark suites that enable a standardized, holistic, and consistent approach to RL testing. We propose a rigorous framework to evaluate and recognize various RL algorithms within this setting. Initial experiments reveal that **P3 off-policy methods** and **on-policy methods** achieve comparable performance across most suites, whereas **P3 on-policy strategies** dominate in others, specifically **LIFLB** and **OBVL**. Furthermore, we observe that **P3 on-policy methods** maintain performance consistency across suite versions, a trait not shared by off-policy approaches which suffer degradation as suites evolve. Finally, we recognize **LIFLB** as a promising emerging direction within RL research. All accompanying code and resources can be accessed at https://github.com/zhongong/L2Explorer.

Process mining has evolved into a data-driven methodology for visually analyzing business processes, leveraging event logs to generate process models that mirror procedural activities. This approach facilitates process improvement by surfacing insights derived from operational data, a capability particularly valuable in dynamic and innovative domains like startups. Such environments often provide only partial visibility into their internal functions, yet they hold significant potential to benefit from process awareness. Although event logging techniques applicable to these sectors have been proposed, they typically focus on explicit, task-oriented actions, which may overlook subtle background operations like communications or system interactions. In contrast, this paper introduces event logging based on continuous streams, a flexible mechanism capable of capturing a broad spectrum of activities, including implicit communications, API invocations, and system errors. By enabling the extraction of event logs through such diverse inputs, this method facilitates the application of process mining to dynamic contexts. Furthermore, it offers mining-oriented exploration and logging tools, along with automatic mining procedures, which streamline the capture of event logs and the subsequent visualization of knowledge.

One-dimensional optical quasicrystals consist of periodic layers whose thicknesses follow a simple linear inhomogeneous recurrence relation, producing a forbidden gap within the photonic band structure. When certain layer pairs swap positions, leading to two possible coupling patterns, we find that these patterns generate distinct, wide localization regions where no states exist even outside the primary band gap. As the linear recurrence relation transitions from a expanding to a contracting regime across the gap, strong coupling between adjacent pairs causes optical states to shift and split into two separate, narrow bands situated inside the gap. We term this phenomenon reentrant delocalization shifting. Additionally, we experimentally construct a 31-periodic sequence of layers, demonstrating a transition of optical shift and observing reentrant shifting behavior that mirrors the theoretical predictions. Finally, we propose a model using coupled oscillators to analyze the system's mechanical response, suggesting feasible methods to engineer and detect similar effects in other physical contexts.

Liger is a new, high-throughput, near-infrared (NIR) imaging detector located at the W. M. Keck Observatory that utilizes parallel data processing. Designed for both night and day operations, it supports scientific analysis, archiving, and quality control. This article details the hardware specifications, along with the data acquisition, retrieval, and reduction systems of the Liger prototype.

This method relies on linearly interacting photons within cavities containing nonlinear media, utilizing a paraxial (bi-photon) interaction to achieve high-fidelity quantum state transfer (QST) between spatial modes. Let $(M, \omega)$ be a symplectic manifold equipped with a compatible complex structure, forming a compact Riemann surface. This work explores two interrelated topics: algebraic extensions of the space of compatible metrics and analytic extensions of the space of complex structures. Such extensions are parameterized by the space of $(0,2)$-tensor fields satisfying specific differential equations. These tensors are either flat under the Levi-Civita connection associated with $(M, \omega)$ or possess a vanishing Nappi tensor relative to it. For complex surface types, the parameterization involves solving a complex Monge–Ampère equation, whereas algebraistic extensions are realized by parallel transport of complex tensors. These extensions are valid for any topological manifold surface, regardless of whether it currently admits a compatible metric or complex structure.

Disruptions in the structural stability of ecosystems often precede substantial shifts in population dynamics, typically manifesting as gradual declines in population growth rates. Although models exist to forecast growth rate collapses, they frequently overlook signs of sudden, rapid population reductions. This study develops analytical methods to forecast both types of downturns within a specific two-timescale ecosystem model. We illustrate how gradual erosion of growth rate resilience parallels statistical indicators of sudden drops. Furthermore, we analyze gradual growth rate improvements as precursors to sudden increases in population growth rate. Consequently, these alternative precursors are identified as effective tools for guiding conservation and management strategies.

Observations show a turnover in the relation between a galaxy's mass and its star formation rate (SFR) at high masses, yet the underlying cause remains unclear. In this work, we evaluate the impact of central supermassive black holes and active galactic nuclei (AGN) by running semi-analytic models with and without such nuclei. Comparisons reveal that without AGN regulation, the $M_{\rm bulge}$-SFR relation fails to exhibit the turnover seen in real data; instead, the relation shifts upward with higher resolution, potentially even failing to display an overdensity at high masses. Conversely, simulations incorporating AGN successfully reproduce both the high-mass turnover and the high-mass galaxy overdensity. Furthermore, while the presence of AGN is necessary to generate the turnover, it alone cannot account for the full magnitude of the high-mass galaxies excess observed.

Cross-lingual sentiment analysis (CLSA) supports consumer cross-border shopping and enhances the stability of international stock markets, yet it remains challenging due to linguistic diversity and data scarcity in languages other than English. Although existing solutions exist, they are largely restricted to English-centric frameworks, relying on manual or semi-automatic transfers for adaptation. This study introduces an automatic approach for CLSA that requires only a single English training corpus and a minimal unlabeled sentence set for each new language. By integrating few-shot name-adapted sentiment label expansion (LSLE) with sentiment label expansion (SLE), the method incorporates sentiment lexicons from the source language into multiple target languages. Furthermore, we developed a multi-task learning (MTC) architecture to construct a comprehensive CLSA model. Experiments across five datasets and three different languages demonstrate that the proposed Multi-Task (MT) model significantly outperforms five state-of-the-art (SOTA) baselines, achieving F1-scores between 40.4% and 68.4%. Additionally, the MTCLN configuration was validated as a strong tool for analyzing international stock markets. The complete codebase is available at https://github.com/zhongyongwang/MTC.

This work introduces two novel operations for stack-based queue selection structures: self-invalidating push (sip) and self-degrading pull (sag). Using these operations, we introduce and examine the multi-priority multi-theft multi-selecting queue (MP-MTQ), which supports $k$ non-negative priorities. Streaming anomaly detection involves identifying irregular data points within continuous data flows, a task critical to numerous real-world applications like network intrusion prevention and equipment health monitoring. Traditional methods often rely on simple statistical measures, such as the Mean Absolute Deviation, to quantify how far data points lie from central tendencies. However, these basic approaches have a key limitation: they offer only basic protections against intrusive anomalies, which can still skew the calculated mean and standardize the deviations inaccurately. To address this, we introduce IQMAD (Incremental Quantum Mean Absolute Deviation), a solution designed for robust anomaly detection that safely handles these disruptive inputs. Beyond its improved safety, IQMAD supports efficient incremental updates, enabling it to process streaming data with minimal computational overhead. Furthermore, we establish theoretical bounds for both true and estimated quantum states within our framework. Through comprehensive experiments comparing our method against existing techniques, we demonstrate that IQMAD not only surpasses competitors in overall performance but also maintains superior accuracy in the presence of intrusive anomalies.

The debate continues regarding whether authorities should mandate encryption, a position many experts support while others oppose. This paper proposes a novel strategy to resolve these tensions: rather than enforcing encryption directly, the government should compel software developers to implement mechanisms for verifying decryption proofs. In this model, users retain full control over their data, allowing them to decrypt it only if a compliant developer has first inserted the necessary decryption verification infrastructure into the application.

Several surface features observed on Jupiter and Saturn, including large spots, jet streams, and thermal anomalies, show rotation periods that do not perfectly match the planet's true spin. This phenomenon is often attributed to the accretion of planets, which alters the core's angular momentum, or to specific mechanisms transporting momentum within the deep interior. We analyzed data from the Juno mission regarding these discrepancies between a planet's actual spin and the period indicated by surface traits. Our approach involved comparing the pre- and post-inferred changes in angular momentum, assuming either an exotic scenario where a planet was consumed or standard models of internal momentum transfer. The results suggest a model involving standard angular momentum transport mechanisms best fits the pre- and post-discrepancies for both the outer layers and deeper regions of these gas giants. Conversely, the hypothesis of planetary consumption requires an implausibly massive object to explain the data. Furthermore, the pattern of non-spinning surface features in the deep interior implies that the planet's interior does not behave as a perfectly rigid body rotating uniformly.

Quantum computing relies on two core mechanisms: long-range valley interference and short-range exchange interactions. While spin swapping occurs through exchange interactions, quantum logic gate operations utilize both long-range interference and short-range exchange. We demonstrate that in silicon, both phenomena can be effectively employed to execute controlled-not (CNOT) gates. Specifically, we execute a CNOT by leveraging short-range exchange interactions to manipulate the Z basis and employ long-range valley interference for this purpose. Additionally, we execute a controlled-phase (CPHASE) gate utilizing only long-range valley interference. Furthermore, we execute a Hadamard gate by combining both methods. Finally, we execute a full two-qubit FermiHubbard model Hamiltonian evolution through a sequence of CNOT gates. Our work establishes a pathway to implement both fundamental mechanisms in silicon, facilitating more efficient multiqubit gate implementations.

Complex adaptive systems, characterized by numerous interacting components that generate non-trivial collective behaviors, pose significant challenges for traditional analytical methods. Addressing this gap, our study proposes leveraging graph neural networks (GNNs) to infer the rules governing such dynamics from data. Since GNN graph convolutions inherently align with causal mechanisms, they enable the learning of rule-based structures directly from time-series observations. We introduce a novel framework that utilizes graph grammars to induce rule graphs from data, which subsequently facilitates the prediction of system states. Testing on a dataset from the Jeopardy! archive, which captures the temporal evolution of topic networks, demonstrates that our method successfully reconstructs the underlying rule graph and accurately forecasts network topology. Furthermore, we demonstrate the system's ability to anticipate the timing of major events, such as rapid shifts in event counts, by detecting corresponding patterns in their corresponding event-like rules.

Adversarial techniques have proven effective in medical image segmentation and classification, yet their application to data augmentation often yields suboptimal results because standard Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs typically fail to capture the full statistical distribution of the images they use. To address this, we introduce the Brain Injury Generation model, an augmentation framework that surpasses typical GANs through a series of successive models. Unlike those before it, our approach does not rely on training a single model across an entire dataset. Instead, it trains separate augmentation instances for both healthy and injured images individually, linking them via a connection that ensures similarity between the two categories. Progressivity is a key feature, allowing the system to refine the complexity of generated anomalies step-by-step by increasing image resolution across cascaded architectures. Furthermore, a collaborative view factor within a dual-variational inference setup facilitates a stronger partnership between damage creation and segmentation modules. Experimental outcomes indicate that enhancing a United States Military Medical Image Segmentation Challenge (UAD) framework with our brain injury generation model significantly improves its performance, increasing the Dice coefficient by 1.3%.

Data collection for the fifth phase of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDS-V) was managed by a federation known as "AstroBots"—a group of six mobile robotic workstations, each controlling four spectrograph data-takers. We illustrate its practical application through a case study of a "gully fill" scenario, demonstrating how this system effectively organized simultaneous searches for two such gullies across multiple robots.

To address these issues, we introduce a novel approach termed "Heterogeneous Group Lasso" (HGL), which models continuous and categorical variables distinctly. Specifically, HGL employs an $l_2$ norm for continuous predictors but utilizes a tailored $\sqrt{l}l_2$ norm for categorical predictors. We demonstrate that a sparse model remains unique and stable under the proposed heterogeneous grouping structure. Furthermore, we derive non-asymptotic bounds for estimation error and model specificity, demonstrating that HGL outperforms existing methodologies in both model selection and parameter estimation. Numerical simulations and real-world datasets substantiate these findings, confirming the approach's practical efficacy. In summary, we provide a robust, unified model that enhances dimensionality reduction capabilities by accommodating both continuous and high-cardinality categorical features with optimized methodologies. We demonstrate the superiority of this heterogeneous framework through theoretical bounds and empirical validation across simulation studies and real-world applications, confirming its efficacy in stable selection and efficient parameter estimation. Numerical results substantiate these insights, confirming the approach's practical efficacy in complex, mixed-data environments.

Passive devices that manipulate linearly polarized light, including isolators and circulators, are fundamental to contemporary optical technologies. Consequently, a microwave-based isolator utilizing this structure is proposed and validated via finite element simulations. This study presents dual-probe rotational Coherent Anti-Stokes Raman Scattering (CARS) sensors operating under femtosecond/picosecond hybrid conditions to measure temperature, pressure, and O₂/N₂ concentrations. By integrating rotational vibrational spectra from both O₂ and N₂, the system enhances temperature and pressure determination accuracy, while the hybrid temporal setup suppresses background noise. Furthermore, utilizing the distinct spectral features of air components in the rotational-vibrational range, the sensor achieves single-shot, simultaneous detection of these species. Experimental results demonstrate high precision for temperature (0.1 K) and partial pressures of O₂ and N₂ (0.005 Torr), with a maximum temperature accuracy of 0.5 K.

The influence of magnetic fields on the development of planetary systems remains a key area of inquiry. Using a magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) framework, we demonstrate that a low-magnitude, negative polarity magnetic field situated within a stellar protoplanetary disk can trigger the creation of two symmetrical, self-perpetuating vortices on either side of the central star. Our analysis indicates that this mechanism operates independently of traditional mechanisms, such as the Kelvin-Tomlinson instability or magnetic kinking. These isolated vortices drive powerful angular momentum extraction, drawing gas inward from the disk toward the central star. Consequently, these structures could potentially initiate early stages of planet formation by organizing the infant disk into distinct regions, while simultaneously acting as barriers to planetesimal migration, thereby facilitating the accumulation of planetesimals into larger bodies. We observe that as the protective disk accretion intensifies, these self-sustained vortices may eventually vanish.

This work outlines the fundamental modeling principles governing hard-drive physics and analyzes their evolution from the 1950s through the 1990s, highlighting key milestones such as pioneering studies by Ahluwalia, Ahuja, Ahuja and Carmona, and our own research group. This paper examines the factorization and resummation of massive quark contributions in exclusive $\gamma^*$+jet production via Drell-Yan. Our results demonstrate that within the widely utilized first-principle tight-binding methodology, stochastic field effects can be transitioned from probabilistic phenomena to deterministic behavior through measure-invariant implementations. This innovative strategy establishes a significant foundation for advancing the computational exploration of complex light-matter interactions.

We investigate the steady-state thermal photoisomerization of a biologically relevant model retinal, specifically 1,1'-bistrimethylammonium-azobenzene (BTA), in the vapor phase using an ultrafast 2D electronic spectroscopy technique. This method employs a pair of consecutive, strongly overlapping femtosecond pulses to probe and drive the molecular system. The initial pulse creates a highly nonequilibrium state, while the subsequent pulse samples it after an extremely short interval, ranging from approximately 2 femtoseconds up to 2 picoseconds. Due to the extreme temporal and spatial overlap of these pulses, BTA molecules are subjected to intense time-dependent parameters, effectively behaving like a molecular oscillator. As a direct result of this reactivity, the molecular systems exhibit a dramatic shift in their relaxation behavior.

Deep-learning approaches have recently gained significant traction in business process mining, specifically for identifying process variants and forecasting process conformance. This study offers a comprehensive review of techniques addressing both variant discovery and conformance forecasting. To evaluate their efficacy in variant identification, this paper employs a dual strategy: it analyzes the algorithms through the lens of unsupervised learning theory and implements all methods using synthetic data to facilitate a direct performance comparison. Additionally, the study assesses deep-learning models dedicated to predicting whether a process will adhere to its specification. Concluding the unsupervised variant analysis, the paper examines supervised learning methods for forecasting conformance, addressing both preparation strategies and the specific scenarios where deep-learning applications are most advantageous. Finally, it presents the results of these experiments and reviews as they pertain to business process mining applications.

This paper investigates the efficacy of utilizing Twitter as a data source for risk reduction initiatives within the emergency response framework. Specifically, it focuses on the September 20, 2020, earthquake that struck Izmir, Turkey, and describes a method for extracting and evaluating tweets related to such emergencies. A key research question examines whether retweeted tweets offer a more reliable indicator of prevalent realities on the ground compared to a comprehensive dataset of all posted tweets. The study compares two datasets: Dataset A comprises the full collection of tweets associated with the Izmir earthquake, while Dataset B consists solely of those with the highest frequency of retweets. Both datasets were analyzed using Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques, including the sentiment analysis framework TextBlob and topic modeling via Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA). The research employs a comparative analysis to determine which dataset yields superior insights. The findings indicate that Dataset B, containing only frequently retweeted content, facilitates a more straightforward understanding of reality than the broader Dataset A, suggesting that for specific research objectives, a curated subset of high-engagement social media data may be more advantageous than the entire dataset.

Periodic photonic structures with PT-symmetry are renowned for their ability to support exotic light-matter interactions. This study presents a theoretical analysis of wave transmission and localized states within a one-dimensional periodic network of $\epsilon$-$\mu$ media exhibiting PT-symmetric non-inversity. We identify three distinct coherent perfect absorption-lasing (CPAL) eigenstates, which emerge in both the PT-broken and unified PT-regimes. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that by tuning the system across the non-inverse transition point, bidirectional transmission can be transformed into unidirectional transmission. In contrast, slight displacement from the bulk states associated with the PT-broken regime yields localized coherent absorption states that function as sensors. Finally, manipulation of the topological phase proves an effective method for creating and controlling CPAL eigenstates, a capability utilized to bidirectionally couple two waves and manipulate their transmission characteristics.

We investigate the dynamics of a capacity-constrained Boolean system on a finite network, incorporating self-interactions and interactions between multiple nodes. By analyzing the growth rate of configuration space and subsequently averaging dynamics within liapounov containers, we demonstrate that these processes exhibit diverse behaviors, including transients, sparse stationary states, and space-filling behaviors, which can transition via a transcritical bifurcation. Furthermore, we analyze a mean-field model in the thermodynamic limit; this model supports an active stationary regime characterized by a non-trivial density that undergoes a transition to either extinction or chaotic dynamics. In particular, we identify a transition to extinction of the percolation type, which is analytically described by a directed percolation model. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the described transitional mechanisms are observable in dynamics governed by VOTM (across various network structures).

This method has been implemented in the ANTOINE codebase. As a proof of concept, we apply this framework to a harmonic oscillator (HO) model, demonstrating the capability to construct a broad spectrum of correlated MQ states beyond the standard HFB limit using these simplified TBMs.

This work evaluates Slotted ALOHA and Carrier Sense Multiple Access (CSMA) access protocols within Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) radar networks. It establishes fundamental properties regarding the number of concurrent detections under CSMA and derives access success probabilities for both CSMA and Slotted ALOHA, incorporating the "blind zone" inherent to FMCW systems. Temporal knowledge graphs (TKGs) encode dynamic interactions between entities across time, serving as a vital resource for domains like biomedical science and social media analysis. Within this context, temporal knowledge graph completion (TKGC) aims to infer missing temporal facts by leveraging entity relations, graph structures, and temporal patterns. A primary obstacle in TKG completion is the alignment between complex temporal patterns and simplistic linear score functions, often resulting in subpar performance. Addressing this, we introduce Temporal Factorization with Low-rank and Model-agnostic Representations (TELLOR), which unifies a broad spectrum of existing embeddings under a single framework. TELLOR integrates a flexible, model-agnostic representation scheme capable of capturing intricate temporal patterns. Furthermore, it employs a low-rank representation strategy to align these patterns with linear score functions, effectively uniting various existing methods. Experimental results on public datasets confirm that TELLOR outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, demonstrating its superiority.

The Jost function method, adapted within the RPA framework, is employed to analyze the prominent Giant Dipolar Resonance observed in $^{16}$O. This theoretical approach accounts for both RPA eigen-energies and direct particle contributions, yielding a comprehensive description that merges them into a single unified formalism. By integrating these elements into the definition of the Jost function, a scattering-related concept, the theory connects the RPA formalism directly to physical observables, thereby facilitating the calculation of charge density distributions. Specifically, this method separates the contributions of RPA states from those of direct particle density. Furthermore, it offers an effective means to sum continuum RPA contributions, which is crucial for ensuring charge conservation. Regarding the giant dipolar resonance in $^{16}$O, this formalism successfully accounts for the phase shifts and the mixing of discrete and continuum states, resulting in calculated form factors that align well with experimental data.

Traditional system identification and clustering methods often rely on assumptions of linearity and Gaussian distributions, constraints that exclude many non-linear dynamical systems. To address this limitation, we introduce an impact-based clustering methodology tailored for such systems. This approach leverages a fundamental property of non-equilibrium dynamics: the tendency of these systems to amplify fluctuations. By analyzing how small perturbations propagate, clustering is achieved by assessing the similarity in their propagator structures. We validate our approach on both canonical linear models, such as the harmonic oscillator, and more complex, exotic non-linear dynamical configurations.

Recent advancements in deep learning have enabled neural language models to achieve significant performance on various linguistic tasks. In this study, we introduce two innovative approaches: an Overlapping Character-level Adversarial Network (OCAN) and a Sparse Generative Adversarial Network for text (SparseGAN). SparseGAN incorporates a sparsification module designed to create high-dimensional sparse high-dimensional spaces that preserve the semantic of the English language. We evaluate our model on a range of natural language tasks, including modeling the unigram distribution of English, generating sentences, and sentence-level classification tasks.

The hypothesis that life can traverse vast interstellar distances to colonize new planets is known as the interstellar panspermia concept. Although this idea remains theoretical, recent technological strides now permit us to model whether current or near-future instruments could identify such life-signs, potentially catalyzing broader societal and scientific discussions. While the subsequent development of life is an inherent stochastic event, the initial delivery mechanism operates under deterministic physical laws. Consequently, by analyzing various cosmic environments, we can map a predictable pattern of survival and degradation for biological entities. In this study, we establish quantitative criteria for detection, accounting for both direct observation and indirect inference through accumulated population densities. Our analysis suggests that microbial organisms traveling at sub-relativistic velocities could reach their destination intact within a few million years—a timeframe achievable by natural phenomena such as supernova shockwaves. Furthermore, with sufficient temporal duration, these signatures would converge within the observable universe, becoming potentially visible via next-generation telescopes.

We utilize disturbance theory to evaluate the impacts of foreground mitigation on the one-point HI intensity power spectrum in future interferometric intensity mapping surveys. Specifically, this study addresses the removal of discrete foreground sources, such as individual galaxies and spiral arms within the Milky Way, which can introduce significant non-Gaussian noise into the power spectrum. Our analysis indicates that neglecting these sources can cause a ~10% error across most redshifts for the target instruments, such as PIMMS and EMIS. However, effective strategies like masking and gridding can substantially reduce this deviation to less than 1%. Conversely, the removal of structure in the Milky Way emission produces larger discrepancies of approximately 10% to 20% at high redshifts ($z > 2.0$). Additionally, the cutoff $k$-mode threshold resulting from foreground subtraction varies by instrument; for PIMMS, the error peaks near the $k$-mode used in simulations, whereas for EMIS, the maximum error occurs at $k$-modes smaller than its typical survey range. These findings highlight the necessity of incorporating foreground disturbance noise when simulating and analyzing data for HI intensity mapping at high redshifts to ensure accuracy.

We introduce a novel statistical framework for animal population estimation that expands the spatial capture-recapture (SCC) model by incorporating animal resource selection. In our approach, animal encounter probabilities are modeled through a two-stage process: first, we estimate the intensity of animal presence at specific locations, and second, we link this intensity to actual detection records to generate posterior estimates of that presence. These SCOR (SpaCe-ReOurce recapture) model components are then applied to produce maximum a posteriori estimates of total population size. We defined this two-stage structure specifically to facilitate the integration of auxiliary data on animal resource use, such as habitat preference, alongside physical capture data. Regarding this auxiliary integration, we identified three distinct modeling strategies, with the leading option being a hierarchical structure that accommodates multiple types of covariates and allows for random effects related to individual animals. We established consistency between SCC and SCOR model outputs regarding total population counts and demonstrated that, under specific conditions, other SCOR models also yield consistent estimates. Finally, we evaluated our methodology through a simulation study designed to compare the proposed hierarchical SCOR model against two competing approaches, confirming its superior robustness and accuracy when and where animal movement or resource use patterns are accounted for.

Although various methods exist to facilitate inter-UAS communication, there is a critical gap in the field regarding research on visual perception and communication protocols for unmanned aerial vehicles. This study introduces a novel visual communication framework that enables information exchange within swarms. The core mechanism relies on the manipulation of lighting colors and patterns on one aircraft's undercarriage, which neighboring aircraft can decode. This system allows non-neighbor aircraft to access information indirectly through a chain of visual "sightings." Key parameters influencing the model include the aircraft's altitude, the precision of its cameras, and the design of the light signals. Within the framework, individual aircraft dynamically adjust their signal patterns based on which neighbors can detect them, whereas each aircraft's camera focus (pan/tilt) is automatically adjusted to maximize the total information acquired from surrounding aircraft. This optimization is addressed using a non-increasing feedback approach, while the information dynamics are analyzed within the context of a time-varying, sparse, and graphical structure. Ultimately, the results demonstrate that this visual framework effectively supports independent situational awareness among the swarms.

The findings reveal that, beyond ring topologies, localization is intrinsically tied to the characteristics of the network's underlying mixing and diffusion mechanisms.

In recent years, numerous polarization indices have been developed to analyze political and social divides, yet they remain frequently applied without adequate scrutiny or justification. This paper examines existing literature on index construction, revealing a common flaw: the failure to distinguish between independent structural distribution effects and the autonomous choice of disturbance thresholds. We demonstrate how separating these components clarifies the proper interpretation of polarisation measures. Specifically, we introduce a structural polarization index that is robustly defensible and can be computed from any existing dataset. We further propose standardizing all comparable polarization indices using a normalization procedure, ensuring their values fall between zero and one regardless of the original measurement scale.

Multilayer networks are frequently modeled as independent layers sharing only interlayer connections, yet in reality, interactions within complex systems often involve overlapping connections where nodes connect directly across different layers. This research investigates the impact of such "transmitting" links on a Kuramoto network of phase oscillators, specifically examining synchronization stability in both sends and receives configurations where an transmitting link substitutes a receiving one. Analytical methods are employed to simplify the heterogeneous multilayer architecture into an equivalent homogeneous system, facilitating the demonstration that homogeneous structural properties significantly dictate synchronization stability. Specifically, we find that the probability of transmitting links influences both the fixed-point solutions and their stability. Notably, the network benefits maximally from these transmitting links when synchronization stability is enhanced. Additionally, it is established that random assignment of these links yields the greatest improvement, whereas non-transmitted (sends) links prove less advantageous than receiving ones.

Software testing is essential for validating a system's correctness, yet generating suitable test cases remains a difficult challenge. This study proposes STAGE, a symbolic execution-based automatic program testing framework that implements a geometric strategy to automatically produce robust test suites. The core idea involves representing the program's execution path as a graph and utilizing the relationship between path constraints and geometric spaces to automatically discover test inputs that traverse execution routes not yet covered. By integrating interval arithmetic with a multi-objective genetic algorithm, the framework maximizes both the quantity of subgraph constraints and path execution length. Consequently, this facilitates the exploration of execution trajectories, thereby enhancing the program's overall testing coverage. Empirical results from a benchmark containing 12 programs demonstrate that the geometric approach successfully identifies inputs revealing novel path constraints and triggers known bugs more effectively than leading state-of-the-art symbolic execution techniques.

We introduce HyperPrompt, a novel framework designed to train prompts for the purpose of conditionally adapting Transformers for multiple distinct tasks. In our approach, task-specific HyperPrompts are generated through a two-stage process. Initially, an off-the-shock prompt is converted into its corresponding HyperPrompt via an invertible transformation applied to each natural language Prompt (NLP). Subsequently, each task is assigned a distinct HyperPrompt using an optimization algorithm. Experimental results indicate that these task-adapted Prompts significantly outperform state-of-the-art performance on six tasks within Natural Language Processing (NLP). Furthermore, we demonstrate that HyperPrompts are acquired in approximately 1/100th the time required by standard prompts, thereby streamlining the adaptation process. Finally, we observe that this adaptation protocol incurs no additional training expenses for downstream tasks. Network scale estimation is a fundamental task in systems like edge computing and data centers, where a leader node gathers distance samples to other nodes to determine the system's size. In wireless environments, links to many peers are constrained by limited transmission ranges, making scale estimation essential for determining reachability. Existing approaches assume hostile actors do not exist, yet in practice, Byzantine faults are prevalent: malicious nodes can emit false distance claims to distort results. This paper introduces a new model integrating network topology, transmission limits, and malicious activity to evaluate estimation accuracy in the presence of adversaries. We analyze how these factors interact and derive a novel, unified framework for assessing expected estimation error. Our proposed model unifies and extends previous topology-based analyses, offering a critical tool for researchers. Furthermore, we introduce SimpleScale, the first scale estimation algorithm capable of handling combined topology constraints and Byzantine faults. SimpleScale employs a randomized, non-exhaustive sampling strategy to achieve robust performance. Experimental results from emulations confirm SimpleScale's efficacy and robustness across various deployment scenarios.

Accurate traffic control and driver information systems depend heavily on the ability to estimate traffic queue lengths with high precision, particularly during traffic signal cycles. This paper proposes a nonparametric short-term estimation method for queues focused on a single lane within an intersection. The approach utilizes nonparametric interval type-2 fuzzy logic (NIFL) inference, combining non-intersecting, non-parametric confidence intervals derived from probe vehicle (PV) positions to model uncertainty regarding both PV position and position variance. By integrating non-parametric short-term estimators, the method processes the interval data to produce queue assessments. The core approach was validated through a Monte Carlo analysis using a representative test case, demonstrating the method's effectiveness in estimating queues under the specified uncertainty conditions.

This lecture provides an overview of fundamental concepts and the terminology central to beam dynamics within accelerator circles, examining how the motion of charged particles around a stable equilibrium evolves. It addresses the effects of linear and higher-order focusing, as well as the theory behind emittance reduction. Additionally, it explores synchrotron radiation within curved trajectories, along with related concepts and language. High-flux neutron and synchrotron radiation facilities are essential for the global research community, facilitating breakthroughs in materials and structural biology sciences. Nevertheless, maintaining and optimizing these resources demands extensive manual labor, which often restricts access to geographically dispersed scientists. To address this, we present an emerging framework of machine intelligence designed to automate core operational tasks, enhance data acquisition rates, and expand geographic accessibility. While general AI advancements are well-documented, the specific computational challenges posed by live data streaming in these facilities have received scant attention. This article details our approach to processing high-performance, time-critical data, which generates massive, precisely stamped datasets. We illustrate how leveraging the Intel® OneAPI Data Analytics suite, specifically its Timestamped Data Extension (TDE), resolves these complexities. This robust processing model simplifies previously intricate operations, enabling efficient handling of extensive datasets that integrate time-series information with structured or semi-structured repository records. Complementing this, we describe machine learning models trained to evaluate the scientific significance of datasets in real time, facilitating rapid, automated decisions on storage, archival, or disposal. Together, these strategies establish a computational foundation for facility operations that supports the continued scientific advancements of researchers worldwide.

Geodesic acoustic modes (GAMs) are prominent in tokamaks, representing a key source of plasma energy loss. This study analytically examines GAM dispersion relations and equilibrium positions in anisotropic plasmas, focusing on the effects of perpendicular and parallel temperature gradients. It is found that such thermal anisotropi significantly alter both the temporal oscillation frequency and radial equilibrium location of the GAMs.

Quantum annealing has been proposed as a method to resolve optimization problems by engineering a system's evolution through varying Hamiltonians. While non-stoquastic Hamiltonians are expected to offer a speedup over the quantum tunneling mechanisms of stoquastic versions, recent studies indicate that they may backfire, leading to outcomes worse than those achieved by stoquastic analogues. We reaffirm this counterproductive behavior by deriving a model demonstrating that, in the presence of local decoherence, quantum annealing speedup becomes achievable even with purely stoquastic Hamiltonians. Furthermore, we establish that strong coupling to the environment is essential for avoiding the backreaction associated with non-stoquastic Hamiltonians. Consequently, speedup generated by non-stroquastic evolution can be nullified, leading to the ultimately disappointing result where the speedup reverts to non-existence or, as our results confirm, the performance drops below that of the stoquastic baseline due to interference effects.

In 1920, the Cambridge Conference established a plan for systematic star cataloging, assigning each galaxy a target area to different astronomers. Kapteyn was designated the supervisor of this project, and in 1922, he founded the "Kapteyn-Arbeidslaboratoriet" (KAL) in Oslo, Norway. This paper chronicles the events leading to the creation of KAL, arguing that despite Kapteyn's reputation as a heliocentric model proponent, he developed a compelling case for a galactic structure based on van Rhijn's observational data. It asserts that KAL arose not merely as a mechanism for overseeing the project, but as a platform for Kapteyn to promote his independent theoretical framework and his growing prestige in Norwegian science, while simultaneously marking a significant milestone in the country's research history.

This framework yields a mesoscale smoothness criterion applicable to domains bounded by a hypersurface with a mean curvature that remains limited, a property previously established by Smoczyk. Deep neural networks (DNNs) continue to achieve significant breakthroughs across diverse fields, driven largely by the continuous expansion of model capacity. As a result, splitting model-parallelism into smaller parallel tasks has emerged as a key strategy for enhancing both training and inference efficiency. This paper presents a new technique for model-parallel training known as Regional Critic Training (RCT). In model-parallel architectures, partial batches are distributed among various layers, yet current methods allocate partial batches statically and uniformly without accounting for data heterogeneity. This lack of awareness can cause performance imbalances during training, as layers process data at differing speeds depending on its characteristics. Traditional solutions, such as synchronous double buffering, only mitigate this issue to some extent and do not eliminate it entirely. Moreover, existing approaches treat all layers identically, ignoring their specific needs. In contrast, RCT dynamically adjusts how partial batches are allocated by first passing a probe batch through the network to gauge the "critic" level of each layer. Based on these metrics, the system then modulates the distribution of subsequent real batches accordingly. Experimental results indicate that using RCT yields a speedup of up to 1.38x over existing state-of-the-art methods.

This research evaluates the capabilities of Electrical Impedance Tomography (EIT) in optimizing the conductivity distribution of conductive polymer nanocomposite (CPN) sensors for impedance-based characterization. The simulations demonstrate that EIT can accurately characterize various damage shapes, a conclusion supported by experimental validation using a physical heterogeneous system. Ultimately, the study concludes that employing a multi-scale EIT configuration is sufficiently precise to enable impedance characterization of multi-phase, heterogeneous damage patterns.

We present a machine learning approach for learning control policies in high-dimensional continuous state-action spaces using very limited training data. This method addresses situations where the data volume is constrained due to the significant costs associated with data collection. Our solution integrates light-weight neural network-based active learning with transfer learning and regularization tailored for continuous states and actions. We evaluate this active transfer learning algorithm in two distinct environments: a simulation of learning flight for a quadrotor and the Atapomatomos walking dinosaur character in Unity. Results indicate the method requires significantly fewer samples than standard active learning to achieve comparable performance. Furthermore, the learning quadrotor is able to follow sinusoidal trajectories in simulation, and the walking dinosaur can mimic its motions within a physical robotic body. Source code for this active transfer learning algorithm and the demonstrated tasks is publicly available at https://github.com/andrew-p-wang/Angle-Active-Transfer-Learning-Control.

Vector spaces are fundamental constructs in mathematics and physics, with Euclidean space representing one of the most significant examples. Within this framework, tensors emerge as essential tools; they facilitate the rigorous definition and analysis of geometric concepts such as vectors, magnitudes, and angles. This study examines key principles related to Euclidean component representation and examines the specific application of metric tensors and inverse metric tensors in these settings. A comprehensive derivation of these concepts is provided, along with an exploration of key properties and proofs of the Gaussian decomposition formula. Overall, this paper serves as a foundational resource in linear algebra and differential geometry.

We examine the feasibility of extending the lifetimes of light flavor-violating particles, specifically those with masses around 1 GeV and Standard Model-like couplings, by enhancing their interactions with either new light particles or increased interactions with dark sector particles. Specifically, we demonstrate that such particles can be made to survive until recombination, with an even more extreme version—accidentally long-lived particles (ALPs)—capable of reaching the end of the cosmic epoch. We establish general principles governing the dependence of particle lifetime on mass and couplings, highlighting a critical phenomenon: enhancing interactions with new light states can simultaneously reduce decay widths and alter momentum dependencies within effective operators. Additionally, we present an operator-based methodology for calculating partial decay widths and validate this approach using an Axion-like particle (ALP) that mixes with a new vector meson of comparable mass, featuring couplings to both visible and dark photons. We further establish constraints on this scenario from cosmic microwave background data and the disappearance of gamma-ray bursts, alongside limits derived from the non-observation of Galactic anti-nuclei. Finally, we propose that future experiments, such as the PANDA facility at FAIR, possess the sensitivity to probe these parameter spaces.

The global pandemic forced a worldwide shift to remote learning, forcing students of all ages to abruptly abandon familiar routines and adapt to new digital platforms and interactions. While prior research examined general academic and psychological effects, there is a critical lack of specific analysis regarding how this transition disrupted student adherence to educational schedules. To address this research gap, we conducted a survey of 100 undergraduate participants, measuring their time management, adherence to routines, and perceptions of routine importance before and after the forced migration to online learning. Quantitative findings indicate a significant decline in time management adherence post-pandemic, alongside reduced adherence to daily routines regardless of their previously perceived value. Qualitative analysis revealed that the constant blurring of boundaries between professional, domestic, and academic environments was the primary driver for these shifts. Ultimately, the study offers insights into specific factors impairing routine maintenance during public health crises, recommending future investigations explore strategies to support routine maintenance within remote learning frameworks.

The study addresses the decoding of lower-body gait phases and step frequencies from electrocorticogram (ECG) signals. Gait decoding holds significant promise for enhancing the usability of current and future artificial limb systems. In this work, we recorded signals from the scalp of an individual performing various gait patterns on a treadmill, with data captured via electrocorticography to ensure high temporal resolution. The primary objective involved determining both gait phases and frequencies across multiple states. We analyzed these signals using both spectral methods and an autoregressive (AR) approach to achieve a decoding accuracy exceeding 99.9%. Furthermore, the results indicate that autoregressive decoding outperforms spectral techniques, demonstrating that high-fidelity decoding of physiological movements like gait is feasible even from high-resolution cortical recordings.

Bayesian inference relies heavily on evaluating the evidence integral, making the thermodynamic integration (TDI) method an essential tool in this regard. This technique determines the evidence by integrating the differential evidence along a path, where each point represents the partition function associated with a hybrid distribution that merges the posterior with any arbitrary prior through a continuous path. While this approach is integral to Bayesian analysis, choosing a hybrid distribution and its trajectory is not unique, and performance can be suboptimal if these are not well-optimized. To address this, we propose using nested sampling to compute the differential evidence. This strategy offers a significant benefit: it allows evidence calculation without the need to define a hybrid distribution or path. Furthermore, the algorithm's efficiency improves substantially by leveraging parallel processing. We demonstrate the method's effectiveness by applying it to calculate the evidence for two distinct models: the virial theorem and the Higgs boson mass.

Graphical models, and specifically Dynamic Graphs (DGs), offer an effective framework for visualizing and quantifying relationships within multivariate time series (MTLS). However, a major obstacle to their broader application lies in the lack of robust, adaptable algorithms capable of reliably estimating Dynamic Graphical Structures (DGS), owing to issues such as limited sample sizes, high dimensionality, and non-Gaussian noise distributions. In this study, we introduce Deep Dynamic Efficient Connectivity (DDEC), a novel black-box methodology designed to infer the DGS from such MTLS. Functioning as a neural-network-based approach, DDEC captures complex temporal and cross-variable dependencies while remaining flexible enough to accommodate various noise profiles. Furthermore, to ensure practical viability, we optimized inference speed by streamlining the computational process. We evaluated the proposed framework using both real-world datasets and controlled simulations, demonstrating that it consistently outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques in both accuracy and robustness.

Phylogenetic networks capture the evolutionary histories of species and other taxa, serving as a natural complement to phylogenetic trees by also reflecting events like horizontal gene transfer and hybridization. Since evolutionary horizontal gene transfer and hybridization are complex, no single event can be captured by a single origin; therefore, researchers develop stochastic network models consisting of probabilistic mechanisms for these combined reticulations and reticulations together with tree growth. Within reticulated networks, we examine three primary classes of generators: pair, single, and standard. In each model, we calculate the probability that a generated network possesses a specific structural configuration. Our findings reveal stark contrasts in how these various models favor networks with different topologies.

Observing biological motion in video is vital for fields like forensics and security, enabling applications such as identifying suspects from surveillance footage or recognizing individuals after a crime. This study introduces a new computational algorithm designed to track human movement by analyzing changes in light and shadow patterns. While human vision naturally detects motion through these subtle visual cues, the proposed system replicates this capability algorithmically. Motility in micro- and macro-scale biological agents, ranging from microbe displacement to organismal migration, stems from localized motility and the subsequent diffusion of surface proteins within their lipid barrier. While crucial, these processes are often complex and difficult to trace experimentally. Although existing tractable mathematical models exist, they frequently omit the link between global movement, individual cell motivity, and protein dynamics. To address a specific subclass of these phenomena, we developed a mathematical framework linking movement to protein diffusion. Our approach utilizes a moving mesh method to simulate how cellular motion alters the affinity of adherent and extracellular matrix (ECM) proteins. By modeling the flow of water through a porous structure generated by moving actin filaments, we created a mathematical representation of motivity-driven flow that causes protein migration across the lipid barrier. Consequently, this framework offers significant insight into biological motivity, paves the way for exploring more intricate scenarios, and could potentially inform strategies for combating infections or cancer.

The public nature of cryptocurrency blockchains enables extensive data analysis focused on understanding currency movement patterns to detect illicit and suspicious activities within the network. Quantum computing relies on fault-tolerant architectures where complex logical operations are constructed from error-correcting basic operations via decomposition algorithms. We illustrate these concepts through two representative systems: a generalized n-level architecture and the 7-qubit distance-3 distance code.

In a quantum Leet two-cavity system, we describe a measurement technique for the quantum phase with high precision, which utilizes a single quantum leet of a two-level atom. This study focuses on the dynamics of hopping robots operating on compliant terrain supported by a single leg. We developed a bi-phasic physical model consisting of vibration-dampening contact and free-air phases to simulate gravity-driven hopping behavior under these conditions. Corresponding equations of motion were derived for both intervals, with the impact transition governed by an inelastic constraint. By solving the resulting hybrid system analytically, closed-form expressions for model states were obtained post-impact as functions of pre-impact states, thereby establishing a discrete, nonlinear discrete-time dynamic map. Simulation results using MATLAB confirmed the validity of both the underlying continuous model and the discrete dynamic map. Furthermore, enhancement strategies for bi-footed hopping robots equipped with elastic storage were explored via modifications to the primary framework within the context of single-leg systems. These improvements enabled the mono-footed model to sustain stable, high-energy storage hopping cycles even when only one leg is used.

We examine the calculation of elastic form factors for both mesons and nucleons at next-to-leading order ($\mathcal{O}(Q^{-2})$) within the framework of covariant one-loop perturbative nuclear and quark effective field theories (EQFT), covering meson production, quark exchange, and light-cone sum rules. Our analysis demonstrates that when higher-twist contributions are incorporated, quark exchange mechanisms dominate the $M_1$ production process, whereas in the elastic scalar ($E_0$) form factor, the quark-meson scattering mechanisms are of comparable magnitude to the exchange contributions. Furthermore, we employ a production approach to derive $E_0$ and $M_1$ scattering in the non-relativistic quark model using a constituent picture, employing a scheme where a specific choice of constituent mass brings these effective field theory calculations into alignment with light-cone sum rules at $\mathcal{O}(Q^{-2})$.

While the behavior of fluids under electric fields is a well-established area of research, inducing turbulent motion in liquids droplet-wise has remained largely unexplored. In this study, we demonstrate, both visually and through theoretical modeling, that rotating rotationally symmetric menisci create complex, three-dimensional EHD turbulence within the droplet form factor. Observations in the atmosphere show that this rotation causes rapid, electric-field-driven evaporation rates, effectively acting as a fan that significantly lowers internal temperatures relative to static menisci. These findings offer a fundamental understanding of liquid transport and thermoregulation mechanisms in the EHD environment, opening avenues for the design of efficient micro-scale cooling systems.

Although NLP systems have advanced to understand affirmative statements, they remain largely ineffective at processing negation, a short yet deceptively difficult linguistic feature. To address this, we introduce CoNDAQA, an open-domain reading comprehension dataset centered on negation and its implications. CoNDAQA presents pairs of contextual passages where one includes a negated answer and either supports or refutes the assertion made by the context, compared to the alternative context which accepts that answer via affirmation. Composed of 4,048 examples from three distinct tasks aimed to evaluate various reasoning capabilities, CoNDAQA remains significantly challenging for state-of-the-art models, yielding low performance metrics. We believe this dataset will be a valuable resource for enhancing natural language inference and negation processing in natural language processing models, and to this end, we release our contextual generation framework which automatically creates these complex dataset scenarios.

We examine how compression and shifting influence the properties of Fock state subspaces. Using these modifications, we determine the maximum possible purity for a single compressed and shifted subgroup state within the (possibly infinite-dimensional) setup. The analysis further explores the dynamics of growth in both subgroup size and spatial dimensions relative to that maximum. Finally, we construct several states—referred to as multiple (n, d)-dimensional state compasses—by leveraging the growth patterns of subgroups within both compressed and shifted frameworks.

The vertical shear instability (VSI) is a proposed mechanism capable of triggering rapid planet formation in the stable annuli surrounding the habitable zones of stellar environments. For this instability to manifest, a temperature gradient opposing the local direction of shear is required; specifically, for disks to support it, dust evolution is proposed to drive the required inversion. However, this work investigates how the longevity of dust grains affects the VSI, challenging the assumption that dust grains instantly migrate to midplane equilibrium. We find that when dust grains do not reach steady state, the magnitude of the induced shear stress escalates, particularly when the stopping time of the particles is either extremely short or extremely prolonged. Although the instability can persist under these non-equilibrium conditions, the magnitude of the generated shear stress is sufficiently potent to account for the observed gaps in disk structures. Consequently, further modeling incorporating the dynamic interplay between hydrodynamics and radiative transfer is necessary to accurately predict where the VSI occurs within protoplanetary systems.

We establish a Liouville theorem stating that a complete, non-collapsed, gradient shrinking Ricci soliton possessing a uniform scalar curvature must be quasi-Einstein; specifically, its curvature tensor $R$ satisfies $R(X,X)=\frac{2}{3}\,s\|X\|^2$ for all vectors $X$. As a consequence, we prove that a complete, non-collapsed, quasi-Einstein shrinking general relative isometric to a Euclidean space or a product of it with a sphere; specifically, it must be the space itself or such a general relative isometric. These findings provide significant contributions towards understanding the structural characteristics and classification of shrinking general relative isometric.

The rise of deep learning has simultaneously spurred targeted attacks on trained models, among which dynamic backdoors stand as particularly insidious. In these attacks, a malicious actor embeds a hidden trap into the model during the training phase by corrupting only a small subset of data, allowing the resulting layer pooling features to expose the infested state. Once deployed, such a model reveals its backdoor only upon receiving a specific trigger input, causing it to produce erroneous or controlled predictions. Although effective, previous approaches suffered from two key limitations: the incorporation of specialized, detectable components and the reliance on extensive retraining for every new backdoor variant. This study introduces two novel, independently viable strategies that enable practitioners to construct dynamic backdoors by leveraging global mean pooling layers found in standard networks, requiring no alterations to the network architecture or additional training overhead. Furthermore, these methods allow the use of existing public datasets to establish the threat. Through comprehensive experiments across various benchmarks, we validate the efficiency of these proposed techniques and demonstrate their success rates.

High-precision astrometry relies on relativistic analysis, where the PPN parameter $\gamma$ significantly influences measured stellar parallaxes. This paper examines how $\gamma$ affects parallax estimates by comparing a gaia-like astrometric model under two scenarios: one where $\gamma$ is fixed at its standard value of 1, and another where it is treated as a free parameter during the fitting process. The study utilizes a gaia-inspired point source model, a white dwarf model, and a binary system model, evaluating performance through Monte Carlo simulations involving $10^6$ trials for each case. Parallax biases and their associated uncertainties were assessed for each model type, revealing that unphysical values of $\gamma$ can cause significant shifts even for fixed values. Furthermore, allowing $\gamma$ to vary freely introduces parallax uncertainties approximately 10% higher than those observed when the parameter remains fixed at its true value.

We introduce a knowledge-driven technique for reducing the dimensionality of dynamical models while preserving accuracy, applicable to both linear and nonlinear systems governed by linear ordinary differential equations with linear or nonlinear coupling. This approach begins with a data-driven discovery of a low-dimensional latent manifold that captures the essential dynamics of the high-dimensional system, utilizing either linear or a combination of linear and data-driven models for embedding. Subsequently, it derives a reduced-order model (ROM) directly from the equations defined on this manifold. This framework yields a coupled mathematical formulation on the manifold and projects it onto a simpler, explicit reduced form. When applied to discovering submanifols in error-tolerant projection scenarios, the method outperforms existing approaches in both superior or equal precision and greater computational efficiency. Furthermore, when utilized within iterative optimization protocols for parameter estimation, it enables rapid convergence to global minima with significantly fewer evaluations, making it ideal for calibrating against empirical data.

We introduce a novel class of multi-solitons termed "self-boosting" because their mutual interactions trigger a rise in their own velocities. We establish a mathematical framework for approximating such solitons at large inter-solititon distances and demonstrate that the self-boosting phenomenon persists within this far-field limit.

This work addresses secure malicious client inference in Federated Learning, a critical challenge where a majority of participants act as adversaries with limited access to model weights, constrained communication channels, and potentially corrupted model structures. While the first-generation Federated Inference with Model Perturbation (FIMP) protocol assumed benign model architectures for attackers, our analysis reveals its vulnerability in those scenarios. To establish stronger security assurances, we introduce a state-of-the-art improvement called Switchable Incremental Multi-head (SIMC 2.0). Beyond upgrading protocol robustness, SIMC also enhances computational and communicational efficiency. Experimental results confirm that SIMC 2.0 maintains a 3.5-norm accuracy within 85% of SIMC 1.0's performance while cutting total computation by 65% and reducing communication overhead by 40%.

Using the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical radio Telescope (FAST), this study conducted sensitive observations of the local universe around the M101 galaxy group centered at redshift $z=0.0369$. The data analysis revealed two extra-planar HI nebulae, designated NEB1 and NEB2, situated approximately 0.6 to 09 Mpc ($c_z$) away from M101. Additionally, clear signs of an HI tail were detected extending from M101's disk on its southern side. An analysis of the HI tail's morphology and physical properties suggests it may have been generated by a ram-pressure event caused by M101 moving through a dense circumgalactic medium. Future research utilizing FAST and next-generation instruments like the Square Kilometre Array (SKA) is expected to discover more unbound HI structures, thereby significantly enhancing our understanding of galaxy evolution and the mechanisms of feedback.

Open-ended Question-Answering (OQQA) measures how well question-answering models display human common sense. In OQQA, candidates must locate a relevant "commonsense" insight from their prior knowledge to derive an answer from three choices. Previous research shows that candidate generation models often rely on superficial patterns in the data to guess answers, which may obscure a deeper focus on actual semantic common sense. This study investigates whether candidates can be trained to utilize genuine semantic-related judgment from the three choices to answer questions in QQA. We discover that a deeper factor exists between the questions and answers in the form of a "story-like" structure. To address this, we introduce CoReQA, a new framework designed to encourage candidates to generate a deeper factor from the three choices to answer questions in QQA. CoReQA consists of two main components: (1) a "story-like" structure induction module that identifies the deeper factor from the three choices to answer questions in QQA, and (2) a careful prediction module that predicts the output based on the identified deeper factor from the three choices to answer questions in QQA. Experiments show that the proposed method outperforms the baseline. The code for CoReQA can be found at this https address: https://github.com/zhongong1993/CoReQA.

Ionized functional groups in organic molecules are frequently linked to the material's chemical reactivity and physical properties. Despite their significance, the cometary spectra of several important oxygen-based molecular cations remain uncharacterized, representing a significant gap in our current knowledge. Addressing this issue, we utilized the RAM-CPS method to conduct *ab initio* calculations on over 1,000 single-codon substitutions for six neutral parental compounds containing oxygen. These parent neutrals were selected based on the volatile species typically observed in comae. Subsequently, we performed molecular docking simulations for these resulting cations against a peptide backbone to model molecular-ion collisions. Our analysis indicates that, with the exception of $\text{CH}_2\text{O}^+$, $\text{CH}_3\text{O}^+$, and $\text{CH}_3\text{OOC}^+$, the vast majority of the characterized molecular-ion cations exhibit large positive HOMO-LUMO gaps ($\ge 0.5$ eV). Furthermore, most function as weaker bases and possess lower electron affinity compared to standard single-cation species like $\text{CH}_4^+$ and $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5^+$. Consequently, these ions are anticipated to display reduced chemical reactivity and produce fewer fragmentations in their mass spectra when interacting with neutral targets.
